decisions.title: Secrets are held behind a handle the door swaps for the credential
decisions.decided_by: Tom
decisions.context: Agents need to use credentials without ever holding them, and revoking access must be instant even for a static key.
decisions.decision: A seat holds a short-lived handle bound to its identity. The real credential sits in the door's encrypted store and never leaves the server. The door's proxy checks SpiceDB, swaps the handle for the credential, forwards the call and writes one audit line. Built in Rust inside the door; no OpenBao unless credentials minted on demand are later needed.
decisions.quote: use something with the service, like a temporary key, and that is then mapped so the actual credential can be used.
consequences: Revoking is dropping the handle, instant for a static key too.
The real key is rotated upstream only when it is suspected leaked.
A key that cannot rotate is still used through the proxy and never read.

decisions.title: The token revolver is the first consumer of the handle
decisions.decided_by: Tom
decisions.context: The workers that run Claude sessions and builders walk their own ordered list of accounts when a session prints its usage-limit words.
decisions.decision: The worker asks the broker for its next account instead of walking its own list; the store keeps the set of real accounts behind one handle and the proxy takes the next in turn and logs which one served each call. This replaces the account pool file.
decisions.quote: that's exactly the kind of thing that we'd want to plug into this, to be able to draw in from there
consequences: Usage is attributed in one place.
Resting an account is a change in the store, with no file copied to any machine.

decisions.title: Everything is pegged to a human authority
decisions.decided_by: Tom
decisions.context: Agents are provisioned under people and act with delegated access.
decisions.decision: A person signs in first; an agent is provisioned under that person with its own identity; the person's permissions are the ceiling and the agent holds an explicit subset; every grant says who may exercise it and who may pass it on; withdrawing the authority stops every grant derived from it. The exact delegation schema is not settled by this decision.
decisions.quote: Basically everything needs to be pegged against the human's base permissions.
consequences: A handle is issued only under a grant that traces to a person.

decisions.title: Manifold is optional and every project stands alone
decisions.decided_by: Tom
decisions.context: The statement names seats being started and ended.
decisions.decision: The engine that starts or ends a seat is whichever one runs the agent: manifold, aion, or a customer's own. Each project in the stack works without the others; an engine without the broker reads its own pool file as it does today.
decisions.quote: It's in the stack as an optional execution engine, but it's not mandatory... I don't want anybody really planning it as a structural cog.
consequences: No broker requirement depends on manifold being present.

decisions.title: The identity database is PostgreSQL, possibly on a network device
decisions.decided_by: Tom
decisions.context: At 14:08 in the Dot room Tom said he had hoped to get rid of PostgreSQL, and asked whether the team thought it was the best solution. The working team decision was one PostgreSQL service and one database for Rauthy and SpiceDB, with separate roles and schema namespaces.
decisions.decision: PostgreSQL is used for the identity product's database. It may be set up on one of the network devices rather than on Tom's Mac.
decisions.quote: Yeah, so we can use Postgres, that's fine. We might just set it up on one of the network devices so it doesn't have to run here.
consequences: Row 02's one PostgreSQL service and database stands.
The host is not assumed to be Tom's Mac; the deployment names its database address as configuration.

decisions.title: A role changes only by a deliberate, explicit act
decisions.decided_by: Tom
decisions.context: Version 4 of the identity mock-up gave roles a builder. At 18:54 on 23 September the room asked Tom whether editing a role changes every holder at once or leaves each holder with the copy made when they got it.
decisions.decision: Editing a role makes a new version of it, and a holder never changes version silently as a side effect of the edit. A holder moves between versions either by a deliberate, recorded act or by an explicit rule shown in advance to the person the holder answers to, such as a move at the holding's next renewal. Which of the two is the default is open. A provisional role is a role held under a grant with an end date: when the date passes the holding lapses, and nothing renews it unless someone grants it again.
decisions.quote: whichever way you went, you'd want it to be deliberate, … and if not deliberate, then explicit … their old lease expires and they don't get a new one
consequences: The role screen shows which version each holder is on, and who still holds an older one.
A holding's end date belongs to its grant, not to the role version: a version change never extends a provisional holding.
A lapsed provisional holding leaves the audit record of its end, and the grants it carried stop at the next check.
Whether a role is a live group or a template copied at grant time stays open.

decisions.title: The product starts an agent by giving its start command, never by running it
decisions.decided_by: Tom
decisions.context: On 22 September Tom settled that the product owns an agent's lifecycle as its record and decision, with a runtime carrying it out (ADR-004). On 23 September at 18:56 he asked how a person actually starts a new agent from it.
decisions.decision: The product is not an execution engine. For the first release an agent's file gives the command that starts it on a chosen machine: the command carries the agent's identity and its handles, never a credential's value, and it is rendered from the agent's kept launch record. A started agent reports back, so the sessions screen shows what is running. A terminal inside the product, sandboxes, virtual machines and containers are later runtimes that plug in, and none is built into this product.
decisions.quote: I don't want this to become like an execution kind of engine … in the first instance, it's starting out with basically like, cool, here's the command that you need to start Waffles
consequences: Every agent carries a launch record: the machine, the runtime, the program, its arguments, the working directory and the handles it needs, by name.

A session is shown running only after the agent reports its start, signed with its own key and naming its launch record; a report that is not authenticated as that identity and that launch record is refused. Copying the command is not a start.
A session that never reports stays unconfirmed.

decisions.title: An agent's file shows its lys certificate
decisions.decided_by: Tom
decisions.context: Reviewing version 4 of the identity mock-up at 18:55 on 23 September, Tom asked that the lys certificate and receipt work be part of the product.
decisions.decision: An agent's file shows its lys certificate once one is issued: what it claims, who signed it, when it was issued and when it expires, with the signed receipts of the changes made to it. An agent registered before any key or proof of possession was supplied shows its certificate as not issued, never a placeholder.
decisions.quote: just making sure that sort of like the original lys certificating stuff is in there
consequences: A change to its grants or role version issues a new certificate; the old one is withdrawn in the log, never edited.
Anyone can verify the certificate and its inclusion in the log offline with standard tools.
Production keys and receipts outside tests remain Tom's acts.
The conformance list checks that a registered agent's certificate, or its not-issued state, and its receipts can be read from its file.

decisions.title: People sign in through a maintained Rauthy fork of our own
decisions.decided_by: Tom (the fork, 14:35 to 14:42); Waffles (its branch and upgrade rule, 15:30:50)
decisions.context: Rauthy v0.36.2 refuses a second provider for a user ('user is already federated'), so linking Google and GitHub to one person needs a change Rauthy upstream is unlikely to accept. Sources: docs/design/identity/STATEMENT-2026-09-22.md:191 (Decided 14:35, Tom); IDENTITY-001 authority (docs/design/identity/briefs/IDENTITY-001.json:10, Tom 14:35 to 14:42; docs/design/identity/briefs/IDENTITY-001.json:17, Waffles 15:30:50) and review_decisions (docs/design/identity/briefs/IDENTITY-001.json:35).
decisions.decision: Rauthy authenticates people, and its one-provider-per-user limit is changed in a fork we maintain, ablative-io/rauthy, not contributed upstream as a prerequisite. The maintained branch is ablative, created from upstream v0.36.2 commit dd61ac3c84d6b238108dc8438b53043b5177a662; the fork's main stays an untouched upstream mirror; lys pins an exact commit of ablative as the submodule vendor/rauthy. Upgrades rebase ablative onto upstream release tags only, each in its own gated row; no cherry-picks and no reset of main.
decisions.quote: The platform keeps its own maintained fork of Rauthy rather than depending on an upstream contribution.
consequences: The fork carries its security fixes for as long as it lives: its maintenance owner is Chippy, with Waffles reviewing security and update decisions (docs/design/identity/RAUTHY-BASELINE.md:39), and the release-and-advisory check recurs before every install (docs/design/identity/STATEMENT-2026-09-22.md:177).
Real sign-in waits on a rebase onto an upstream release carrying both hardening commits, the separate future brief IDENTITY-002 (docs/design/identity/briefs/IDENTITY-001.json:462-473).
A change inside the fork belongs to the fork's own repository: a brief of this repository names such a file with its owner and never lists it as its own file.

decisions.title: Every product shares one design and keeps its own accent; the identity product's is orange
decisions.decided_by: Tom (15:18, 15:20 and 15:21:43), relayed by Waffles (15:19 and 15:21)
decisions.context: Tom asked for a consistent design across the products and named Aion's browser appearance as the one he is happiest with; Cambium is not yet the reference. Sources: docs/design/identity/STATEMENT-2026-09-22.md:194; IDENTITY-001 authority (docs/design/identity/briefs/IDENTITY-001.json:14-15) and review_decisions (docs/design/identity/briefs/IDENTITY-001.json:43-44).
decisions.decision: The identity screens follow Aion's structure, typography, spacing and interaction, and Rauthy's client themes take the same colours, with no build dependency on Cambium or Aion. Each product keeps its own accent within the estate colour family: Cambium green, Aion blue and black, Argus light blue, Haematite mustard. The identity product's accent is orange (accent #D4975A, deep #A86B2E, wash #3D2A17 in the estate colour tokens), set apart from Manifold's copper. No product is silently made Aion-blue, and purple is not used.
decisions.quote: Every product shares one design and keeps its own accent.
consequences: Rauthy's pages carry our colours and corner radius only; their fonts and layout stay upstream's (docs/design/identity/STATEMENT-2026-09-22.md:191).
Exact accessible light and dark accent values are declared and reviewed before a theme is accepted.
Whether one design system is extracted for every product is not settled by this decision.

decisions.title: An identity is registered, active, suspended or retired
decisions.decided_by: Archie, for the working team (proposal of 17:10); not ruled by Tom
decisions.context: Tom, 17:08, put identity, access, permissions and the start of lifecycle management before everything else (docs/design/identity/STATEMENT-2026-09-22.md:183). Archie proposed these states so the directory has something to register an identity into; the document calls itself 'a proposal for the room, not a settled design' (docs/design/identity/LIFECYCLE-STATES-2026-09-22.md:1-8).
decisions.decision: An identity is in one of four states: registered (exists in the directory, no grants, no credential handle, may not act), active (may act within its grants), suspended (kept whole, grants kept but not effective) and retired (permanent, history kept, never reactivated; a new identity is made instead). Register, activate, suspend, reinstate and retire are the only transitions, each one signed audit record naming the authenticated actor and their provenance, the identity, from, to, when and reason. Having a grant or a credential is a fact beside the state, not a state. A person is registered by first sign-in; an agent is registered by a signed-in person, who carries it as its responsible person for life and may cause every transition of their own agents. Source: docs/design/identity/LIFECYCLE-STATES-2026-09-22.md:17-44 and docs/design/identity/LIFECYCLE-STATES-2026-09-22.md:71-95.
decisions.quote: We got to talk about identity access management, permissions, and the start of lifecycle management before we get to the nitty gritty of the lifecycle that we're actually managing
consequences: DIRECTORY-003 records the state beside each identity; no check reads it until the permission work of road step 2.

The room's own questions stay with the proposal: whether a reason is mandatory on suspend and retire, and whether activation needs a credential handle (docs/design/identity/LIFECYCLE-STATES-2026-09-22.md:101-103).

decisions.title: A compaction's loss is a lys.loss custom entry beside it, and a session's block hashes are a lys file beside the session
decisions.decided_by: The lead who owns the home compaction card (RM-006), answering its survey
decisions.context: A compaction stored beside its original must say what it could not keep, and a listing must be able to check that every summarised entry and block is still held. Pi's grammar has no place for either (home DESIGN P2), and no home entry records which blocks it came from: the importer's store_part discards the hash BlockStore::put returns, and message entries keep their parts inline in Pi's shape, so re-hashing a part does not give the stored block's hash.
decisions.decision: Each compaction entry is followed in the file by a lys.loss custom entry, a side leaf under the compaction, whose data names the summarised span's first and last entry ids, its counts of entries, messages, tool calls, tool results and blocks, their bytes, a digest of the span's block hashes and the harness's tokensBefore, deterministic so two imports agree apart from ids and timestamps. Block hashes are kept in <id>.blocks.jsonl beside the session, one {entry, part, hash} row per stored part, as the index and head are kept. Rejected: a new field on a Pi message or a custom entry per message for block references, which adds to Pi's grammar or doubles every import's entries; re-hashing parts or following only harness-event record hashes, which cannot find the stored blocks; and placing the loss entry on the chain, which would re-parent the record after the compaction and break the importer's parent equality.
consequences: RECORD.md's list of lys.harness_event kinds grows to six; the five existing kinds and the 512-byte data cap do not change.
The session gains an append that does not move the head and a head hash: the SHA-256 of the head entry's line.
Claude Code's transcript slot is filled by resuming the rendered file by path with --fork-session, so the rendered file is never written after the render.
A use-only secret is only ever its handle; a readable secret is refused until the secrets rows build the broker reader, whose command mapping the template carries as text.
Each further harness is its own template and its own measurement; manifold, the door and aion may consume the printed line and none is a dependency (ADR-004).
RECORD.md carries lys.given's data shape beside the other lys custom entries.
A later change to the shape is a new custom type or version alongside, never a mutation of lys.given, once anything is signed over it.
Settings, hook output, plugin skill and agent listings and output styles are recorded by later cards as further kinds on this same entry shape.
A check of a file against the record is by hash only, and prints neither file.
HOME-002 lands the proof with findings recorded one per line, each carded, and leaves the seven cards in review while any finding stands on their rows.
A card carrying a row with no code at the commit measured (HOME-001 R7, R10) stays in review marked not built until that row is built through the chain.
Every other row built before the chain needs its own proof card before its card can be done.
RECORD.md documents both entries with their data keys; a change to either is a new custom type alongside, never a mutation of the shipped one.
Appending lys.fork to a parent takes the parent's one-owner lock and rewrites no earlier byte (home P1).
The render skips both entries, as it skips every custom entry, so neither reaches a Claude Code file.
RECORD.md names lys.loss, its fields, its place and its span rule, and tells it apart from a render's .loss.json.
A session imported before the block rows existed is reported by the listing as unverified, never guessed at.
The span is walked by seeking through the index, never by reading the whole session file (CN7).
HOME-002 delivers it.

decisions.title: Claude Code's compaction is read and rendered in the shape the measured version writes
decisions.decided_by: The lead who owns the home compaction card (RM-006), answering its survey
decisions.context: HOME-001 R3 maps Claude Code's summary record to a compaction entry and R4 renders a compaction as that summary line. Measured across the compacted Claude Code files on one machine, there are 3,415 compact_boundary system records, each followed by an isCompactSummary user record, and one summary record; a boundary becomes a harness event and its summary a plain user message today, and the rendered summary line leaves the summary in no record the model reads. Home DESIGN P6 makes a resume path a per-harness, per-version measurement, never an assumption.
decisions.decision: The importer reads a compact_boundary record and its isCompactSummary record as one Pi compaction entry: the summary is the isCompactSummary message's text, the first kept entry is the entry of preservedSegment.headUuid (the compaction itself when there is no preservedSegment, so it keeps nothing), tokensBefore is compactMetadata.preTokens, and Pi's details field names both source records by uuid; a named first kept entry not on record is refused by uuid. The summary record path stays for the file that carries one. The render writes a compact_boundary record, then the isCompactSummary record, then the kept records, with the parent chain advancing through all three, measured on the installed Claude Code version. Rejected: attaching the loss entry only to the summary record path, which almost no file uses, and keeping R4's summary line, which a resumed session would not read.
consequences: RECORD.md carries lys.given's data shape beside the other lys custom entries.
A later change to the shape is a new custom type or version alongside, never a mutation of lys.given, once anything is signed over it.
Settings, hook output, plugin skill and agent listings and output styles are recorded by later cards as further kinds on this same entry shape.
A check of a file against the record is by hash only, and prints neither file.
What the four rules report on lys code is a finding, recorded as its own line and carded; mod.rs files carrying logic are reported by a check, not by an author's eye.
The rule set is not yet a leg of .land/gates.sh; wiring it into the gate is its own unit.
HOME-001's checklist row C3 says the compact_boundary pair is R3 corrected by measurement.
HOME-001's R4 text is amended to name the measured render shape, and its render fixture is updated.
Older compacted sessions without a preservedSegment import as compactions that keep nothing.
HOME-002 delivers it; a later Claude Code version that changes the shape needs its own measurement.

decisions.title: A lantern is a custom entry in its session, and its note grows only by epilogue entries
decisions.decided_by: The stage 5 lantern request, which names the record shape; recorded with HOME-004
decisions.context: Stage 5 of the home needs lanterns: a note plus a point in a transcript, declared on purpose, that a later session or a fork walks back to. The home record is Pi's session tree and lys adds entry kinds only as custom entries (home P2, CN4). The shape chosen here is the one the stage 5b fork will cut from, so it has to be fixed before anything is lit under it.
decisions.decision: A lantern is a `lys.lantern` custom entry appended at its session's head, carrying in custom.data the entry id of its point (an existing entry of the same session that is not itself a lantern or an epilogue, the head or any entry the head has moved past), the note as written, who lit it and when. Its note grows only by `lys.lantern_epilogue` custom entries naming the lantern's entry id and carrying the further words, who added them and when; a lantern's story is its entry followed by its epilogues in order, and nothing is rewritten. Rejected: Pi's `label` entry on the target (it replaces or clears a label rather than growing one, and carries no author or time), a lantern store beside the session outside Pi's grammar (a lantern would stop travelling with its session), and editing the lantern's note in place (the record is append-only, P1).
consequences: HOME-004 defines both custom types and documents their data fields in docs/design/home/RECORD.md.
Lighting appends at the head, so the head moves onto the lantern; the stage 5b fork cuts at the lantern's point, never at the head.
A lantern or epilogue is never a lantern's point; adding to a lantern is an epilogue.
Entry ids are unique only within a session, so an epilogue and a recall by point always name the session with the id.

decisions.title: A lantern's note and epilogues are the person's annotations, not transcript
decisions.decided_by: The lead of the home card, answering the stage 5 survey
decisions.context: Home P7 and CN3 forbid transcript contents in output, logs and errors. A lantern's note is written as a line of the session file, and recall exists to print it, so the principle and the stage 5 request conflicted until it was settled whether a note is transcript.
decisions.decision: A lantern's note and its epilogues are the person's own annotations, not transcript. Recall prints them by design; they are the one exception to P7 and CN3, and only recall prints them. Transcript lines (message, tool and compaction content) still never appear in output, logs or errors, and a recall row never carries a line of the transcript around its point. Rejected: treating notes as transcript and printing only their hashes, which makes recall useless to the person who wrote them.
consequences: P7 and CN3 of docs/design/home/design.json are amended with HOME-004 to state the exception.
The lys-home README and RECORD.md say that lantern notes and epilogues are the one text the crate prints, and only recall prints them.
Errors from lighting and epilogues still name no note, epilogue or transcript text: ids, paths and counts only.

decisions.title: A rendered file's derived uuids are a fixed, versioned contract
decisions.context: The Claude Code render gave every entry id that is not uuid-shaped a fresh random uuid, so two renders of one session head differed and no hash could name a rendered file; the launch template then shaped one from the SHA-256 of the entry id alone, deterministic but outside any namespace, without a role, and equal for the same entry id in any two sessions. Deriving those uuids from the record under a fixed scheme makes a render deterministic, and from the first receipted render event onward a hash names a rendered file, so the derivation fixes those hashes the way a wire format fixes signatures. The fork and launch cards need the same kind of derived id.
decisions.decision: Derive every uuid a render needs and the record does not hold as UUIDv5 under the session's namespace and the name `<entry id>#<role>`, with a closed set of roles (`record` first); the session's namespace is UUIDv5 over one fixed lys namespace (32c05904-d1f1-550c-9eee-2f6c8f98b665, itself UUIDv5 of the RFC 9562 URL namespace over `lys/home/claude-code/render-uuid/v1`) and the id of the session being rendered, so the same entry id in two sessions never derives one uuid. Treat the namespace, the session namespace rule, the name form and the roles as frozen: a change is a new version alongside, never a mutation. The fork and launch cards derive by this scheme. Rejected: drawing fresh ids (nondeterministic), keying on a hash of the entry id alone without a namespace, a role and a session (two roles on one entry collide, two sessions with one hand-authored id collide, and it is not reproducible with standard UUID tooling), mixing in the target session id (the record does not hold it), and leaving the scheme mutable until a later card (every recorded hash would move with it).
consequences: HOME-007 implements the derivation for the role `record` and pins a fixture hash in PROOF-RESUME.md.
A fork or launch card that needs a derived id adds a role to the closed set, never changes the namespace, the session namespace rule or the name form.
Changing the derivation breaks every recorded render hash and is written as a new version with its own namespace, alongside the old.

decisions.title: A fork is a child session cut from the parent's own lines at a lantern's point, with its ancestry on both sides
decisions.decided_by: The stage 5b fork request and the lead's answers to its survey; recorded with HOME-006
decisions.context: A lantern is a pathway back to a conversation with the self that lit it, and Claude Code resumes a session only from its end. The home record is Pi's session tree (P2); Pi's own fork writes a new session whose header's parentSession is the source file's path and copies the source entries. The fork has to say which session a lantern was lit in, since a copied line keeps its id and a child holds a copy of every lantern on the copied chain.
decisions.decision: A fork resolves a lantern to the session it was lit in, read from the lys.lantern data's lit_in when the record carries it and otherwise by the older-record rule (one holder cuts, several refuse lantern_ambiguous until a session is named), and cuts that session's root-to-point chain at the last assistant message at or before the point, through the index. The child is a new session under the parent's cwd whose header's parentSession is the parent file's path relative to the home, holding each cut entry as the parent file's own line bytes, then one lys.forked_from custom entry as its head naming the parent session, the lantern, the point, the cut entry, whether the coordinate was carried and the carried entry; the parent gains one lys.fork custom entry at its head naming the child. Nothing else is copied and no block is written. Rejected: re-serialising the copied entries (the copy would stop hash-matching the parent's lines), a fork store beside the sessions outside Pi's grammar, cutting at a point no lantern names, and a header field beyond Pi's parentSession.
consequences: HOME-006 defines both custom types and documents their data in docs/design/home/RECORD.md; a copy of a lantern's line in a child is a copy, never a second lantern.
A lantern that sits before any assistant message is refused nothing_to_fork: a point before the first reply would carry only a seed, which is a new session and not a fork.
The fork report carries ids and counts only: entries copied, distinct block hashes the copied entries name that the store holds, and those it does not.
The lantern card records lit_in in a later round; until it does, every lantern the light act writes resolves by the older-record rule.

decisions.title: A user-message point is carried as a seed prompt beside the rendered file, never copied into the child
decisions.decided_by: The lead's answers to the fork survey; recorded with HOME-006
decisions.context: A lantern may mark a user message. Copying it into the child would leave the child ending on a question no reply answers, and dropping it would lose the coordinate the lantern marks. The measured cut of the lantern design carries the message as the first prompt instead.
decisions.decision: When the point is a user message the cut stops at the assistant message before it and the message is carried, not copied: lys.forked_from records its id with coordinate_carried true and counts, by kind, the parts of it that are not text. The Claude Code render of such a child writes the message's text parts, in order, as a seed prompt beside the rendered file under an in-band marker line naming the parent session, the point and the lantern, and names it in the render report; the template's launch line, printed by render-launch only, passes that file as the resumed session's first prompt. A part that is not text never refuses a fork or a render and never enters the seed. Rejected: copying the user message into the child's chain, refusing a fork for a non-text part, and putting the seed's text in the report or the loss account.
consequences: The seed lives only in the render's output directory, as the rendered JSONL does; the report, the loss account and the fork entries carry counts and ids.
A seed path that already exists is refused by name and the render writes nothing.
The launch line is printed, never run (ADR-007); the proof runs it by hand and records which line it ran.

decisions.title: A root is a repository URL and a pinned commit, resolved through the worker's own checkout and never fetched
decisions.decided_by: Archie, lead for lys, in the rulings on the roots card's rounds
decisions.context: lys's docs/design/project.json names the estate's other projects by absolute directories on one machine, which no worker on another machine resolves, while the carded-row rule is that workflow inputs name a repository, a commit, a card and a brief, never a folder. The method's reader accepts only absolute directories today, so the shape and the reader must change in a stated order.
decisions.decision: Each root in project.json is an object with repository, a remote URL, and commit, the full hash of the commit the design was checked against. A worker resolves it through DS2_CHECKOUTS/<last URL segment without .git>, which must hold the commit (git cat-file -e), and otherwise is refused by name with the checkout path, the repository, the commit and the act of fetching that commit into that checkout. The repositories map (project name to remote URL) is retired into root.repository, so a root's repository has one home, and the method's validator refuses a project.json that still carries it, by name, naming the move to root.repository. The pin moves by hand in a gated row. A check prints each root's pin beside origin's head and the distance between them, and exits 0 whatever the distance; a root whose checkout lacks its pin is reported as pin_absent with the act git -C <checkout> fetch origin, a root whose checkout has no refs/remotes/origin/HEAD is reported as origin_head_unset with the act git -C <checkout> remote set-head origin --auto, and either makes the check exit 1, only after it has reported every root. The resolver and the check import only the Python standard library and SDK-free modules of ds2_ledger, so lys's copies run under python3 from a fresh clone. Rejected: keeping absolute directories; a resolver that fetches or clones what is missing; following the moving head or moving pins automatically; a pin per design; a lys-local resolver; and unifying the roots map with the $NAME/ launch tokens in this card.
consequences: lys's project.json does not change shape until the method's reader accepts the object; ROOTS-001 R2 is blocked on that method commit and first refreshes lys's copies from it.
The resolver and the pin check are written in the method, on the design-system board, and lys receives them only as copies.
A survey reads the pinned commit, never the moving head, so a stale pin is visible and moving it is a gated, stated act.
The project.json files of aion, cambium, haematite and the design system follow on their own boards once the method accepts the shape.
A project.json that still carries a repositories map is refused by the method's validator until its entries move into root.repository.

The leg-entry reading project.py takes from venues moves into an SDK-free ds2_ledger module, legs.py, which lys copies beside project.py; the pin check's copy differs from the method's only in the line that finds workers/, which SOURCE.md names.

decisions.title: A certificate carrying one claim is revoked whole, by its issuing authority's key, permanently, by a leaf folded in lys-identity
decisions.decided_by: The lead for the identity line, in answer to the certificate revocation card's survey rounds; recorded with DIRECTORY-013
decisions.context: DP26 (docs/design/lys-anchor/DECISIONS.md:400-425) rules that revocation is an append and the live set a fold, that the revocable unit is the claim unit, and that the freshness tolerance is a verification input with no default and N in the answer; it is recorded only in the lys-anchor decisions and was never built (docs/design/identity/STATEMENT-2026-09-22.md records it as ruled, not built). Building it for certificates left open what is revoked when a certificate can carry several claims, who may sign a revocation, whether a revocation can be undone, which history must still verify after one, what a revocation of a certificate the log does not yet hold means, where the code lands while lys-core calls revocation a consumer concern, whether it discharges DIRECTORY-006 R4, and whether the published no-log verification changes meaning. This entry records that build in the project ledger; DP26 stays where it is and is the proposal this entry records.
decisions.decision: A certificate carries one capability claim, so the revocable unit and the claim unit are the same; revoking a claim is revoking its certificate and issuing a new one without it, and the fold never treats a certificate carrying several claims as partially revoked. Only the issuing authority's key signs a revocation leaf; a person responsible for the agent under ADR-003, or an administrator, revokes by asking the directory, which asks the authority to append, and the fold refuses a revocation signed by any other key. A revocation is permanent: no leaf reinstates a certificate, the fold refuses a reinstatement leaf by name, a verbatim replay of an earlier issuance leaf included, and the way back is a new certificate. A revocation always names a certificate the log already holds: the fold refuses a revocation leaf with no earlier issuance leaf for its certificate as revocation_before_issuance, and a later issuance of that certificate is valid. A revoked certificate's inclusion and consistency proofs and its issuance record always verify, and an attestation by its key verifies if and only if its own log entry precedes the revocation leaf, the log order being the evidence of time; an attestation with no entry before the revocation leaf fails, naming the revocation leaf; an attestation by a certificate that is not revoked needs no log entry of its own. The fold and the revocation-aware verification live in lys-identity; lys-core keeps revocation a consumer-side non-goal, and its published verify_certificate_chain and the lys ca verify command keep their meaning and keep passing with no log, while a new library form taking the log, the size N and the tolerance as explicit inputs checks revocation; its command line is a later, separate unpublished binary, and the published lys binary does not depend on lys-identity. Certificate revocation and grant revocation are separate folds: this stands beside DIRECTORY-006 R4 and does not discharge it, and C25 stays open with DP26 as the proposal its review reads. Rejected: revoking claims one by one inside a certificate, letting any key but the issuing authority's sign a revocation, a later leaf reinstating a certificate, letting every attestation made before a revocation stand whatever its log position, a revocation standing for a certificate the log does not hold, building the fold in lys-core, and changing what the published no-log verification means.
consequences: DIRECTORY-013 builds the fold, the append, the verification and the history calls in crates/lys-identity/src/revocation/ and its code rows block on DIRECTORY-003 having landed, checked by the crate existing on main.
The certificate-log leaf formats are a new wire format, signed only in tests until the repository's constructed-attack review of them is recorded.
The typed-claim card issues one claim per certificate; no format revokes part of a certificate.

lys ca verify's help and lys-identity's documentation say that verification without a log does not check revocation; lys-core's published rustdoc of verify_certificate_chain does not, and the act that answers that gap is a documentation-only lys-core release, its own card.

The revocation request path, through which a person responsible under ADR-003 or an administrator asks the directory server and the issuing authority signs and appends, is a later unit blocked on DIRECTORY-006 R4 and on the directory server; until it lands the only way to revoke is a caller that holds the issuing authority identity.
A command line that revokes or verifies against a log is a later unit, a separate unpublished binary.

The directory design's step-2 non-goal and CN11 each gain one appended line naming DIRECTORY-013's revocation fold and history check as step-2 work brought forward; the rest of each stands as written.

decisions.title: The fork's ablative branch moves only from a green candidate, with its previous head kept under a tag
decisions.decided_by: Archie, lead for the identity line, in rulings on the Rauthy release rebase card (RAUTHYREBASE-001)
decisions.context: ADR-009 says upgrades rebase ablative onto upstream release tags, each in its own gated row, which means force-pushing ablative. Every earlier lys commit pins an exact ablative head as its vendor/rauthy gitlink, so a force-push can leave that head unreachable and break recursive clones of history; a rebased head pushed straight to ablative can leave the branch on a head that does not build; and a fork migration can share a number with an upstream one without any textual conflict.
decisions.decision: Before any force-push of ablative, its previous head is pushed under a tag naming it (pre-rebase-<old base tag>-<short sha>). The rebased head is proved first on a candidate branch rauthy-rebase/<new upstream commit>; ablative is force-pushed with --force-with-lease naming the tagged previous head only after the fork build and full suite pass there. A failure on the candidate moves nothing and keeps the candidate branch; a later failure in the same card resets ablative to the tagged head with --force-with-lease naming the rebased head, verified by ls-remote, and stops by name. Before the rebased build, the postgres and hiqlite migration numbers of both sides are listed, and a number held by both stops the card naming both files and the upstream commit; it is never renumbered to fit. Rejected: force-pushing the rebased head straight to ablative and proving it there, force-pushing without keeping the previous head reachable, and renumbering a colliding fork migration.
consequences: Amends ADR-001's placement of the broker inside the door; ADR-001's handle model is unchanged and its entry is not edited.

The entry is decided by the owning lead as a technical decision, not by ADR-001's decider, because only the broker's placement moves and the handle model Tom decided in ADR-001 is unchanged; each code row's Blocked by check tests that the entry is decided.
Every SECRETS-003 code row's files sit in the lys repository, under crates/lys-secrets.
CN4 of the secrets design is answered by this entry; SECRETS-002's open reading of the host is closed by SECRETS-003 without editing SECRETS-002.
The cambium paths SECRETS-002 names are not walls for any row; no cambium file is edited for the broker.

The entry stays proposed until Tom gives his word, and then moves to decided with decided_by set to exactly ADR-001's decided_by value, `Tom`, and his word cited in its context; each code row's Blocked by check tests that equality.

Every SECRETS-003 code row's files sit in the lys repository, under crates/lys-secrets, and every code row carries Tom's word on this entry in its own Blocked by; if he keeps the broker inside the door, those rows' file lists are re-briefed as an amendment before any is dispatched.
CN4 of the secrets design is answered by this entry once it is decided; SECRETS-002's open reading of the host is closed by SECRETS-003 without editing SECRETS-002.
lys-proxy keeps R10's own behaviour and records partial or unrecorded as its spec says.
A test on forward.rs asserts the error kind on a refused connection and that no response bytes are invented; a test on the example asserts the 502.
If the rule is ever wanted for lys-proxy too, it is a change to R10's contract, stated there, not a change made under the example.
Both payloads are reviewed adversarially with the envelope before any durable byte is signed under them, and are frozen from their first signature; a change is a new version alongside.
The card waits for DIRECTORY-003 R2 and for lys-log-store 0.3.0.
lys open stays the verifier and writes nothing.
Entries of other kinds (lys.given, lanterns, forks, messages) are not signed by this.
The directory refuses linking a person's provider account to an agent and delegating a sign-in identity, each by name and writing nothing (DIRECTORY-009).
An agent's own machine account, bound to no person, stays allowed as its issuer-subject binding (conformance row 1.3).
The broker refuses to issue an agent any credential derived from a person's sign-in session; this is carried by the broker's card against SECRETS-002, and row 1.2 is met in full only when it passes.
Every earlier lys gitlink stays reachable through its pre-rebase tag; a pre-rebase tag is never moved or deleted.
ablative is never left on a head whose build and full suite have not passed.
Every push of ablative names its lease, so a fork commit pushed while a rebase runs fails the lease instead of being dropped.
A fork migration takes a number after upstream's highest at the commit it is rebased onto; a collision is a stop, never a fix-up.

decisions.title: The home's non-goal on signing narrows to anchoring
decisions.decided_by: The signed entry log request; recorded with HOME-008
decisions.context: The home design held anchoring, signing and receipts into a lys log out of scope until asked for. Signing lys.call entries, lys.harness_event entries and sealed-record opens into a lys log under the identity has now been asked for, with anchoring, encryption at rest and Haematite named out of scope.
decisions.decision: Signing into a lys log is in scope for lys.call entries, lys.harness_event entries and sealed-record opens, and for nothing else; anchoring stays out of scope. Rejected: keeping the whole non-goal, and widening signing to every entry kind.
consequences: No new signed format and no new version beside lys/delegation/v1 is written for the lease.
v1's lack of not_after is recorded as a fact; the lys-identity grant's window is the limit a lease is checked against.

These criteria wait on the grant's window, defined by DIRECTORY-006 R1 and enforced at admission by DIRECTORY-006 R4: SECRETS-002 R9 acceptance criteria 5, 8 (SEC_LEASE_ATTENUATION) and 10 (SEC_PROVISIONAL_EXPIRY), SECRETS-002 R7 acceptance criterion 8 (SEC_REINSTATE_CURRENT's expired handle), and SECRETS-003 R3's lease-window refusal leg.
A window carried in a signed delegation stays open, as SECRETS-002 records it, and would be a new version alongside v1.
A lease a stranger verifies offline, if a later row needs one, is a new brief with its own adversarial review.
The home design's first non-goal names anchoring and every other entry kind, not signing as such.
lys.given stays unsigned (ADR-013).

decisions.title: A lantern records the session it was lit in as an optional typed lit_in; a lantern without it is an older record resolved by its holders
decisions.decided_by: The lit_in card's request and the lead's answers to its survey; recorded with HOME-014
decisions.context: ADR-014 fixed what a lantern carries (its point, the note, who lit it and when) and not the session it was lit in, and ADR-017's fork has to know that session, since a copied line keeps its id and a fork's child holds a copy of every lantern on the copied chain. The light act recorded no lit_in, LanternData refused the key as unknown, and the fork read it from the entry's raw data as a stopgap, with fixtures writing a lit_in lantern by hand. Lanterns lit before this change carry no lit_in, some carry no lit_at either, and none can be rewritten to carry it (P1).
decisions.decision: LanternData gains an optional lit_in, the id of the session that held the point when the lantern was lit, and keeps refusing unknown keys; a present null and a present non-string value are kept distinct from an absent key. The light act writes it as the id of the session at whose head it appends the lantern and reports it; recall reports it beside point, note and lit_by, as null for a lantern whose data has no lit_in, and gives a lantern whose lit_in is present and not a session id the fork's lit_in_not_a_session refusal with the fork's reason text, skipped by note and refused by point, never a row and never entry_shape. The fork reads lit_in through a narrower typed view carrying point, lit_by and the optional lit_in, which requires neither lit_at nor note: a lantern whose data has no lit_in is an older record and resolves by its holders as ADR-017 rules (one holder cuts, several refuse lantern_ambiguous until a session is named), and a lit_in that is present but is null, not a string, not a safe session name, or names no session of the home is refused lit_in_not_a_session naming which, never read as any session. Rejected: making lit_in required (every lantern lit before it would become the wrong shape, skipped by recall by note and refused by recall by point); refusing a lantern with no lit_in by name (every lantern lit before it would become unforkable, retiring ADR-017's older-record rule); reading a null lit_in as an absent one (a silent fallback to the holder rule); the fork reading the full LanternData (the older records without lit_at would stop being forkable); and rewriting earlier lanterns to carry it (P1).
consequences: HOME-014 adds the field to LanternData, the light act, its report and recall's rows, switches the fork to the typed view, and documents lit_in in docs/design/home/RECORD.md.
ADR-014's lantern shape is extended by one optional key, not replaced: a lantern lit before HOME-014 is read as it is and stays forkable.
ADR-017's older-record rule stays in force for a lantern with no lit_in; retiring it is a separate decision.

The fork's fixtures light with the light act every lantern it can produce, and write by hand only the records it cannot: a lantern with no lit_in, a copy whose lit_in names another session, and a malformed lit_in, each named in its test as such.
Once lanterns are lit under it in a real home the shape is frozen; a change to lit_in's meaning is a new version alongside.

decisions.title: The Rauthy client themes are dark only from the estate tokens, and every field the estate names no token for is a named gap
decisions.decided_by: The lead's rulings on the DIRECTORY-002 themes; recorded with DIRECTORY-002
decisions.context: DIRECTORY-002 R3 asked for all seven HSL fields, button text and border radius of both Rauthy client themes in light and dark mode, but the estate colour tokens name only a dark foundation (ink, surface, raised, text, muted) and each product's accent. They name no light mode, no error colour, no radius, no emphasised text tier, no action colour, no text-on-accent and no per-mode icon, so filling every Rauthy field would mean inventing colours the design system never chose.
decisions.decision: Both client themes are dark only. A Rauthy field takes an estate token only where the estate names the same role: the dark text takes text, bg takes ink, bg_high takes raised and accent takes the client's product accent. Every other field is a gap that keeps Rauthy's own default: light mode, the error colour, the radius, and the dark text_high, action, btn_text, theme_sun and theme_moon, eight in all, listed by name in deploy/identity/theme-map.md. Rejected: mapping text to muted, which would set the body of every page in the secondary colour; and choosing colours for the fields the estate names no token for.
consequences: deploy/identity/rauthy-themes.json sets only the dark text, bg, bg_high and accent of each client; the light fields, the dark error and the radius stay as Rauthy holds them.
deploy/identity/theme-map.md names the eight gaps, and nothing reads a gap.
A design-system card that names tokens for the gaps fills them; until then each keeps Rauthy's own default.

Readable contrast is measured, not asserted: WCAG 2.1 AA over named pairs, a gap field measured at Rauthy's own default; a gap field whose default fails over ink stays a gap and stops the row by the pair's name, and the fix is a token the design-system card names.

decisions.title: The home translates a session imported from Claude Code into a Codex rollout: one admitted pair, a fork with a loss account and a side leaf
decisions.decided_by: The lead's answers to the translation survey; recorded with HOME-009
decisions.context: The home design listed harnesses other than Claude Code as a non-goal, and ADR-012 rejected a transcript converter per harness for the launch template. Roadmap stage 4b asks for the first translation as one named pair with its own account. Codex's own importer of Claude Code files is a compaction and not a copy: it drops thinking, sidechains and meta records and clips tool calls to 2,000 and tool results to 4,000 characters. Without a ruling the card would contradict its own cluster, and the fork would either repeat the importer's losses or claim to be the session it came from.
decisions.decision: Admit exactly one derived harness pair, Claude Code to Codex, as stage 4b, rendered by the home as a fork of the session, the same act the Claude Code render performs, for a second harness. Every text part, tool call and tool result is carried whole as Codex's own items; readable thinking is carried as text and opaque blocks are dropped (P3); a base64 image is carried as Codex's input_image item and an image of any other source is listed lost, never fetched; a sidechain is carried as marked text under the turn that spawned it; a branch summary or custom message on the context path, each of which feeds the model's context, is carried as marked developer text under its own marker, as a compaction is; a child forked at a user message carries that message's text after the walked history as the thread's next user prompt, the continuation's first prompt, read through seed_of from the parent session's file, the one file read beyond the session's own, each of its parts that is not text listed lost; entries a compaction leaves off the context path are listed lost naming the compaction; a message of any other role and a tool call or result with no id, name or call id are listed lost, never given an empty default; harness events, lanterns and other lys entries, render records included, are listed lost. The in-band marker names the source session id, the source head hash and the Codex version, the same three the account carries, and no template hash, since no launch template takes part. A JSON loss account beside the rollout lists kept, changed (with before and after kinds and the fields in how) and lost (with a reason) by entry id and the hash of each part as the home entry holds it; a tool_use's caller field, dropped at import, is recorded nowhere yet and is a later card's to record; and a lys.translation custom entry beside the context path records each translation. The thread id is record_uuid of the session head, so the Codex thread is a fork and never the same session, and its durable link back is the account and the side leaf, not the in-band marker. The recording and the resume run in a scratch Codex home outside the repository, logged in with the proof account, a Codex login named by its role, by the card's lead seat and never by the chain's builder, never the live one, and no credential file is copied. Rejected: adopting, wrapping or calling Codex's importer; listing sidechains as lost; writing into the live Codex home; copying an auth file into a scratch home; treating the Codex thread as the same session; recording the translation as a seventh lys.harness_event kind; a template hash in the marker; reading each part's stored block, with a refusal when it is not stored.
consequences: The home design's non-goal on other harnesses admits this one measured pair and no other; Chat Completions or Responses translation, Pi and every third harness stay out of scope.
ADR-012's rejected per-harness transcript converter stays confined to the launch template, which never converts a transcript; launching Codex through a template is that template's next version.
The translation never moves the head and never writes a byte of the Claude Code render, so the Claude Code render of a translated session is unchanged by hash.
The account and the report carry ids, hashes, kinds, field names and counts only (P7, CN3).
Each head translates to a new Codex thread; a Codex continuation never comes home.

decisions.title: A Codex rollout's shape is a per-version measurement, and the translation refuses any Codex version but the one measured
decisions.decided_by: The words of the translation card; recorded with HOME-009
decisions.context: Codex's rollout format changes between releases: rollouts written on the proving machine by 0.155 and 0.156.0 carry line-level ordinal keys and item metadata that the June source checkout does not, and a thread Codex cannot read resumes silently wrong or not at all. P6 already makes a resume path a per-harness, per-version measurement.
decisions.decision: The translation writes the shape measured from rollouts Codex 0.156.0 wrote, confirmed by a recorded 0.156.0 fixture and a resume on 0.156.0, and refuses any other --codex-version by name, telling the caller to render for 0.156.0 or card a measurement of the new version. Rejected: assuming the shape from Codex's source checkout, accepting a version by prefix, and rendering an unmeasured version on a best-effort basis.
consequences: Each new Codex version is its own measurement card before the translation accepts it.
The time zone that names a rollout's directory and file is an explicit input, and an unnamed or unknown zone is refused with the words set TZ to an IANA name.

decisions.title: A handover is a rule-less lys.inherited entry and the letter's turn copied whole into a new successor home, its inheritance read from its first entry
decisions.decided_by: The lead's answers to the handover survey; recorded with HOME-015
decisions.context: HOME-001 R12 describes the handover, and the tree contradicts three of its sentences. An imported Claude Code turn holds its signed thinking and its text as separate entries, so one entry id cannot carry both. Pi's session_info carries only a name, and CN4 forbids lys data outside custom.data, so session_info cannot hold an inherited field. The canon's Inherited type requires a rule, a letter is not a rule, and the canon reader never reads an example's data today, so making the rule optional would let a rule-less example into the canon unrefused.
decisions.decision: The letter is one or more entry ids, a run of assistant message entries standing next to each other on the outgoing session's path, in path order. Each entry is copied whole, keeping its id, its timestamp and its message, with only its parent link rewritten to chain onto the successor, and from_entries lists every id in that order. The successor is a new home directory, absent or empty, holding one new session with a fresh id, the outgoing header's cwd and no parentSession. Its first entry is a lys.inherited entry with no rule, then the copied entries, then a session_info whose name is `inherited from <outgoing session id>`, and no field is added to Pi's grammar. The first entry is what says the successor's first memory is inherited; the handover's own report reads it from there and prints inherited true, and the render report and its count of canon examples are unchanged. The canon loader newly refuses by name a canon example whose lys.inherited entry has no rule; a lys.inherited entry in a session of a home is read without that check. Rejected: merging the run into one message (composing the letter), copying one entry (half a letter), a session_info flag (breaks CN4), writing into the outgoing home, and setting parentSession, which ADR-017 keeps for a fork's ancestry.
consequences: A handover writes nothing when it refuses, and the outgoing home is only read. Every refusal is taken before the successor directory is created or written.

A letter entry that is not an assistant message, a run that is not contiguous on the path, an entry whose message carries provider `authored`, and a run with no thinking block are each refused by name, naming the entry. A successor path that holds anything is refused by name.

Inherited.rule is optional in the type and skipped when absent, so a canon entry with a rule serialises to the same bytes as before; canon add and a render with --canon refuse a canon holding a rule-less example.
Launching a successor from its handover through the launch template is a later unit; HOME-002's template gains no slot here (ADR-012).

decisions.title: lys enforces its code rules with ast-grep, recognising test code by structure the file carries
decisions.decided_by: Archie, lead for lys, in the rulings to the ast-grep card's runs 04213a71, 0d44242f and 6747ce61; recorded with LYSCORE-003
decisions.context: The lys gate had no ast-grep leg, so its rules against unwrap, expect and panic outside tests, against lint bypasses, against dropped Results and against logic in mod.rs held only where clippy overlapped them. Cambium's rule set carries no unwrap rule and forbids every #[allow], while lys CLAUDE.md sanctioned a per-module #![allow] opt-out for tests. An unwrap rule has to tell test code from library code, and 224 calls at 4dd1c33 sat in fixture.rs files and in helper fns of *_tests.rs files, none of which carried an in-file test marker.
decisions.decision: Carry Cambium's mod-rs-declarations-only, no-let-underscore-on-results and no-lint-bypass-attributes, and add lys's own no-unwrap-expect-panic-outside-tests. That rule treats as test code a file whose first item is #![cfg(test)], a #[cfg(test)] mod body, a #[test] fn body, and a path under tests/. Every *_tests.rs file, both fixture.rs files, every integration test root and both tests/harness/mod.rs files gain #![cfg(test)] as their first line. The per-module #![allow] opt-outs are replaced by clippy.toml's allow-unwrap-in-tests, allow-expect-in-tests and allow-panic-in-tests. Every existing hit is fixed at its cause in the same card, so the leg is green when it lands. The leg `ast-grep scan --config sgconfig.yml` runs in docs/design/project.json, .land/gates.sh and CI. Rejected: an exemption list of file names; rewriting the calls in test files; narrowing no-lint-bypass-attributes to spare the test opt-outs; carrying only the rules that were clean at the time.
consequences: A new sibling *_tests.rs, fixture file or integration test root begins with #![cfg(test)], or the unwrap rule reports its helper calls and clippy refuses them.
No #[allow] remains in the tree; an #[allow] outside tests is fixed at its cause, and one that cannot be is brought to the lead as a question with its line.
CLAUDE.md and Cargo.toml name clippy.toml in place of the per-module #![allow].
Every carried rule is at severity error, and the leg fails the gate on any hit.
The leg needs a gate venue that declares tool:ast-grep.

decisions.title: A rule that cannot fire on the lys tree is not carried
decisions.decided_by: Archie, lead for lys, in the rulings to the ast-grep card's runs 04213a71, 0d44242f and 6747ce61; recorded with LYSCORE-003
decisions.context: Cambium's set includes no-std-mutex-in-async and two door-timer rules. At 4dd1c33 lys has no async fn, no tokio and no std Mutex, and the door-timer rules are limited to Cambium door-handler paths. Rules that cannot fire would report zero hits forever and look like cover, and a control that never fires cannot be told from one that passed.
decisions.decision: no-std-mutex-in-async, no-timer-in-door-handlers and no-timer-import-in-door-handlers are recorded as not carried, with that finding. The card that lands the first async code in lys carries no-std-mutex-in-async with it, and its brief names this decision. Rejected: carrying all six of Cambium's rules because the words said the same rule set.
consequences: The first card to add an async fn or tokio to lys adds rules/ast-grep/no-std-mutex-in-async.yml in the same card and cites ADR-064.
The door-timer rules stay out of lys while it has no door handlers.

decisions.title: The hand-written lys-core documents are kept as *-PRE-METHOD.md, not replaced by the method's render
decisions.decided_by: Archie, lead for lys, in the rulings to the ast-grep card's runs 04213a71, 0d44242f and 6747ce61; recorded with LYSCORE-003
decisions.context: docs/design/lys-core held a hand-written DESIGN.md, CHECKLIST.md and USER-STORIES.md from before the design method. Once the cluster gains a design.json, the method renders markdown under those same names and the design gate compares it byte for byte, so the render would overwrite the earlier design.
decisions.decision: Before this cluster is rendered, the three documents are renamed to DESIGN-PRE-METHOD.md, CHECKLIST-PRE-METHOD.md and USER-STORIES-PRE-METHOD.md with their bytes unchanged, and the method's render takes the old names. The live citations of the old paths are re-pointed to the new ones. LYSCORE-003's card is the one owner of docs/design/lys-core. Rejected: overwriting the documents with the render, and deleting them.
consequences: The pre-method documents are read, never edited.
Other cards write nothing under docs/design/lys-core.

decisions.title: The given statement is a lys/attestation/v2 over the RFC 8785 bytes of lys.given's data, written only when render-launch is given a key
decisions.decided_by: The lead's rulings on the given-statement card; the canonical form chosen by HOME-016's author and proposed with that brief
decisions.context: CONFORMANCE row 6.5 asks that what an agent was given be a signed statement checked with lys verify --attestation. The lys.given entry records the hashes of the documents a session was given and no hash of itself, lys-core's attestation signs SHA-256 of a payload, and a signed form is frozen from its first signature, so the bytes signed have to be named so a stranger can rebuild them with standard tooling.
decisions.decision: The given statement is lys-core's existing lys/attestation/v2 over the RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme) bytes of the lys.given entry's data, so its signed payload hash is the given hash render-launch reports as given_sha256. It is written only when render-launch is given a key: kept as a block named by a lys.given_statement entry hung under the lys.given entry, and as given-statement.cose and given-data.json under --out for lys verify. Rejected: serialising the record in struct field order, which a stranger cannot rebuild without the Rust type; signing the 64-hex hash string, whose attested hash would be SHA-256 of the hex and not the given hash; adding the given hash to the template_render event, which HOME-003 keeps unaltered; and changing lys verify's one failure message to name the file, which would change the published lys for every user.
consequences: The RFC 8785 form of lys.given's data is a wire contract from the first signature; changing it means a new statement type alongside, never a mutation.
A render with no key writes the lys.given entry as HOME-003 records it and no statement, and says unsigned.
The statement is checked with the unchanged lys verify; which key signed is checked by comparing its signer public key with an expected key until row 6.1's --cert checks it against a certificate.
The start statement and the role-move statement are later statements over the START launch record and the ROLES version record, written when those records land.

decisions.decided_by: The lead's rulings on the given-statement card; the canonical form chosen by HOME-018's author and proposed with that brief
decisions.context: CONFORMANCE row 6.5 asks that what an agent was given be a signed statement checked with lys verify --attestation. The lys.given entry records the hashes of the documents a session was given and no hash of itself, lys-core's attestation signs SHA-256 of a payload, and a signed form is frozen from its first signature, so the bytes signed have to be named so a stranger can rebuild them with standard tooling.
decisions.decision: The given statement is lys-core's existing lys/attestation/v2 over the RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme) bytes of the lys.given entry's data, so its signed payload hash is the given hash render-launch reports as given_sha256. It is written only when render-launch is given a key: kept as a block named by a lys.given_statement entry hung under the lys.given entry, and as given-statement.cose and given-data.json under --out for lys verify. Rejected: serialising the record in struct field order, which a stranger cannot rebuild without the Rust type; signing the 64-hex hash string, whose attested hash would be SHA-256 of the hex and not the given hash; adding the given hash to the template_render event, which HOME-003 keeps unaltered; and changing lys verify's one failure message to name the file, which would change the published lys for every user.
consequences: The RFC 8785 form of lys.given's data is a wire contract from the first signature; changing it means a new statement type alongside, never a mutation.
A render with no key writes the lys.given entry as HOME-003 records it and no statement, and says unsigned.
The statement is checked with the unchanged lys verify; which key signed is checked by comparing its signer public key with an expected key until row 6.1's --cert checks it against a certificate.
The start statement and the role-move statement are later statements over the START launch record and the ROLES version record, written when those records land.

decisions.title: The gate's test leg runs every test binary; it never stops at the first failure
decisions.decided_by: The gate test-leg card's words and its lead's answers; recorded with LYSGATE-001
decisions.context: The gate's test leg runs cargo test over the workspace with all features and without --no-fail-fast, so it stops at the first failing test binary: a run that fails in one crate reports nothing about the binaries and crates after it, and a gate can go red for one reason while hiding others. project.json's legs are copied verbatim into every new cluster's gate, so the fail-fast form spreads with each cluster.
decisions.decision: Every declaration of the gate's test leg runs `cargo test --workspace --all-features --no-fail-fast`: project.json, every cluster design.json gate, .land/gates.sh and CLAUDE.md's 'Gates before any commit' block; CI's test step gains the same one flag and nothing else. Rejected: keeping cargo's default fail-fast run, which is shorter on a red round but reports only the first failing binary.
consequences: A new cluster's gate copied from project.json carries --no-fail-fast.
A red test leg runs every test binary before it exits, so a red round holds the build venue's battery lock longer than a fail-fast run did.
The leg still exits non-zero when any test fails; no timeout is raised and no test is split to compensate.
--no-fail-fast does not continue past a compile error, so evidence that every binary ran comes from a planted test that compiles and fails.

decisions.title: A carded row built before the chain is done only when the chain has judged its code at a named commit and no open finding touches its files
decisions.decided_by: The lead's rulings to the chain-judgement survey; recorded with HOME-008
decisions.context: HOME-001's built rows reached main by hand before every carded row had to go through its board's chain, and the seven step 5 cards that carry them sit in review with nothing on main saying the chain judged that code. Setting them done on the merge alone would make done mean merged; setting them all done on a green landing of a proof would make done mean the proof landed, whatever it found.
decisions.decision: A carded row built before the chain is set done only when the chain's whole judgement has been run over its code at a named commit and no finding still true on current main touches that row's files; a row with an open finding stays in review, pointing at each finding card, until they close. Green means the landing passed src_pr and src_land, never that the code is clean. Rejected: setting the cards done on the merge alone, and setting every card done when the proof lands green regardless of its findings.
consequences: resolve_given lists appended_instructions and mcp_config ahead of user_claude_md, and the lys.given data shape of ADR-013 is unchanged.

RECORD.md states the one rule and names the old order as superseded by the commit that lands HOME-011 and its date; a reader tells an entry's order by comparing its recorded time with that date, and never by its harness_version.
A later harness card records its documents in the order its harness's request gives, and a harness-side input the request carries no trace of takes its place from the read order until it is measured.
A card that measures a real MCP server's tools position fixes mcp_config's place by that measurement.
A session, canon or fork child holding an entry the render cannot shape no longer renders; the refusal names the entry to repair and nothing is written.

Sessions the importer wrote with a redacted_thinking part that carried no data hold thinkingSignature null and now refuse to render; the importer's own defaults are the other half of the defect and belong to the importer card, not to the render.
A session holding an aborted turn does not render until the Claude Code format has a value for it.
The bytes rendered from a session that carries every field do not change, so every pinned render hash stands.
Supersedes HOME-003 R2's rule that the template's CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR names the config directory, on a no answer, for the Claude Code version measured.
The decision is accepted with the measured answer and the Claude Code version it was measured on; a yes answer leaves lys.given as the record and lys.given.v2 unwritten.
The config-directory rule is re-measured on each Claude Code upgrade, as a resume path is (home P6).
The judgement is measured on a checkout of the named commit and recorded against its sha, apart from the landing's own gate and its sha.
Each finding is its own line; one answered on main names the fixing commit and gets no card, one still true becomes its own card.
A row whose files are not on main at the named commit is not judged and its card is not set done.

decisions.title: A home moves as one fast-forward git ref pushed to a path on this machine, tracking exactly its record stores
decisions.decided_by: The lead's answers to the move survey; recorded with HOME-019
decisions.context: Stage 3 of the context roadmap moves a home by a pushed ref the target fetches, never a hand copy, with encryption before any bytes leave the machine as its precondition. A home holds, beside its record, lock files and temporaries that must never travel; its blocks hold imported tool results verbatim and a template's env and mcp slots are free strings, so no scan can promise a home holds no secret; and git's own settings can change bytes on the way in or out.
decisions.decision: A home directory is a git repository whose tracked files are exactly each session's file, index and head, each block and each template, enumerated by name and never by pattern; the first ship initialises it. ship holds every session's lock through its check and snapshot, commits that set, and pushes it without force as the one ref refs/lys/home to a bare repository at a path on this machine, creating it when the path does not exist; a remote ref the new commit does not descend from is refused as ref_diverged. Every other remote, ssh to any host, https, git or file URLs and hosted services, is refused as remote_not_local until stage 3's encryption exists. git runs as the binary with a pinned environment and no filters. Rejected: an allow-list of estate ssh hosts, scanning the home for secrets, a pure-Rust git crate, and force-pushing or overwriting a ref.
consequences: No byte of a home leaves this machine through ship until the secrets step's encryption lands; the second-machine block fetches this ref after that.

A home with no session, a stale or missing index or head, a session a live owner holds, a repository tracking other files and a remote path that is not a bare repository are each refused by name before anything is pushed.
The gate machine needs git on PATH.

decisions.title: An arrival is a seventh lys.harness_event kind, one per arriving session, hung beside the head
decisions.decided_by: The lead's answers to the move survey, and the lead's answer that fetch commits the arrival; recorded with HOME-019
decisions.context: Stage 3 gives the target a distinct execution id with its ancestry recorded, and the identity documents describe an execution per session or fork. The source is never written, so the ancestry can only be written on the target side, and the arrival is a fact about the record, not a turn.
decisions.decision: fetch appends to each arriving session one lys.harness_event of kind arrival whose detail carries the source commit, the remote, the ref and a fresh execution id for that session's continuation. It hangs beside the head through append_beside, as template_render does (ADR-012), so the head file, the head hash and the next render's session_head on the target are the source's. fetch then commits the appended entries as one commit whose parent is the fetched commit, naming the source commit, the remote and the ref, so the target's git status is clean and a later ship from it carries the arrival onward; a failed append or commit removes what fetch created. There is no home-level id file and no block is stored for it. Rejected: an arrival that moves the head, arrival lines left uncommitted until the target's next ship, one execution id per home, and a block for the arrival's data.
consequences: A target's head file is byte-identical to the source's after fetch, and a render of the target records the source's session_head.
A remote whose arrival data would pass the 512-byte cap is refused before fetch writes anything.
The target's HEAD is one arrival commit on the fetched commit, and a ship from the target carries the arrival to the next home.

decisions.title: A home moves as one pushed git ref of an allowlisted tracked set, never a hand copy
decisions.context: Stage 3 of the context roadmap moves a home off the machine that captured it, by the route a build tree takes: a pushed ref the target fetches. A home holds session files, their index, head and lock files, the block store and the template store, and blocks hold raw request and response bodies. Copying the directory by hand carries lock and temporary files, has no commit to name what moved, and leaves no ancestry; tracking the whole directory carries whatever else lands in it. The shape is decided before stage 3's second block fetches it from another machine (docs/design/home/briefs/HOME-004.json).
decisions.decision: A home is a git repository whose tracked set is an allowlist: sessions/<id>.jsonl, <id>.index.jsonl and <id>.head, the files under blocks/ and the files under templates/, never a lock, temporary, environment, render or execution-id file. `lys-home ship` commits exactly that set with git run apart from the person's configuration and pushes it without force as one ref, refs/lys-home/<commit>, to a remote named on the command line; `lys-home fetch` fetches that ref into a new home. Rejected: a hand copy or an archive of the directory, which names no commit and records no ancestry; tracking the whole directory, which ships whatever else is in it; and a pure-Rust git crate, which adds a dependency where the git binary suffices. Until encryption at rest exists, ship refuses a remote off this machine and any tracked file holding a value of the named secret values file or matching one of five standard secret patterns (private key header, sk- token, GitHub token, AWS access key id, JWT).
consequences: RECORD.md names the tracked set, the ref namespace and the home's own branch refs/heads/lys-home.
Ship and fetch check an index and a head without rebuilding either, so a source home is never written outside .git/ and a target refuses rather than repairs.
Stage 3's second block fetches this ref from another machine, and the off-machine refusal is lifted by the encryption-at-rest card, not before.
A later change to the tracked set is a decision alongside this one, since a fetched home depends on what was shipped.

decisions.title: An arrival is a seventh lys.harness_event kind, hung beside the head and written by fetch
decisions.context: A fetched home must record where it came from and carry its own execution id, so that its ancestry is on the record. The lys.harness_event kinds are a closed set of six, and ADR-012 rejected advancing the head for a record the model never sees, because it moves the session head hash and splits renders of one session. This extends the closed kind set and adds execution identity to the home, so it is written down on its own (docs/design/home/briefs/HOME-004.json).
decisions.decision: Fetch appends to each session one lys.harness_event of kind `arrival`, with source_uuid and record null and a detail of exactly source_commit, remote, ref and execution_id, hung beside the head with append_beside so the head and the session head hash do not move; the execution id is one per target home, fresh at fetch, kept in the untracked file <home>/execution-id. The remote is recorded as a canonical path, a file:/// URL, or a URL without userinfo, and the data stays within the 512-byte cap. Rejected: appending the arrival on the context path, which moves the head (ADR-012); a new custom entry type, which adds a type where the harness event carries the same shape; and one execution id per session, where the words give the home one.
consequences: RECORD.md lists arrival among the lys.harness_event kinds with its four detail keys.
No importer maps a harness record to the arrival kind; only fetch writes it.
