A render of a fetched home carries the same session head hash as a render of its source.
A remote that would push the arrival past the cap is refused at fetch before the target exists.

decisions.title: A translation to another harness is a per-target, per-version renderer of our own with a loss account, never that harness's importer
decisions.context: The home promises that a session can move to another harness, and translation had been designed and not proved. Codex already ships an importer of Claude Code files; measured in the lantern work (tools/lantern/docs/02-SESSION-FORMATS.md section 3), it is a compaction and not a copy: it drops thinking, sidechains and meta records, clips tool input and tool results, and records no account of what it dropped. The ruling recorded there was to improve on it and not adopt it. The first pair, Claude Code to Codex 0.156.0, is built in HOME-004, and every later pair (Codex to Claude Code, Pi) will face the same fork, so the shape is decided once.
decisions.decision: A translation to another harness is a renderer of our own, one per target harness and per measured version, over the home's context path: it carries every text part, tool call and tool result whole as the target's own items, carries readable thinking as text and drops opaque blocks by hash (home P3), announces itself in band as a translated context naming its source session and head hash, writes a JSON loss account beside its output listing kept, changed and lost by entry id and block hash, and is recorded on the session as a side leaf. It is not the target harness's own importer, adopted, wrapped or called, because that importer is a compaction that loses what the home keeps and cannot say what it lost; and it is not one renderer for every version, because a harness's file shape is a per-version measurement (home P6).
consequences: Each target version is measured from files that version wrote before it is rendered for; an unmeasured version is refused by name.
Every translation writes a loss account whose block hashes key to the home's block store.
Every translated thread carries an in-band marker naming its source session and head hash.
The target harness's importer is never a dependency and its code is never copied.
Later pairs (Codex to Claude Code, Pi) are their own renderers under this rule, each proved on its own.

decisions.title: Audit receipts are for changes only; answered permission checks go to step 2's separate access record
decisions.decided_by: Waffles, the lead, at 22:56 on 26 September 2026 (W1); recorded with DIRECTORY-007
decisions.context: The audit receipt card asked whether a permission check that is merely answered, not changed, leaves a receipt. Every signed receipt is a leaf in the lys log in operation order (docs/design/identity/briefs/IDENTITY-001.md:49); a check is answered many times a minute once step 2 enforces anything, so putting answered checks into the signed receipt log would make it a high-volume access log that drowns the changes it exists to prove.
decisions.decision: Receipts are for changes only. A check that is answered and changes nothing is not a receipt. When step 2 brings enforcement, allows and refusals go into a separate access record that step 2 defines: refusals are always recorded there, and whether allows are too is decided with step 2. Rejected: every answered check as a signed receipt in the lys log, and deferring the question to the build.
decisions.quote: Receipts are for changes only. A check that is answered and changes nothing is not a receipt.
consequences: DIRECTORY-007 writes this as a boundary and as constraint CN15 of the directory design, so nobody later puts high-volume checks into the signed receipt log.
Step 2's access record is a non-goal of DIRECTORY-007; the brief that brings enforcement defines it and decides whether allows are recorded.
In step 1 nothing answers a permission check (CN11), so the only receipts are the listed changes and the directory service's sign-ins and sign-in refusals.

decisions.title: The receipt verifier lives in the lys CLI, offline, needing only the log and the service's public key
decisions.decided_by: Waffles, the lead, at 22:56 on 26 September 2026 (W2); recorded with DIRECTORY-007
decisions.context: The audit receipt card asked where the verifier lives: the lys CLI or the directory service. A verifier is what a party holding only the log and the key uses to check the directory's history without the operator's cooperation (story S7, DIRECTORY-003 R2's read-only verification path).
decisions.decision: The verifier lives in the lys CLI, as lys log verify receipt, offline, needing only the log directory and the service's public key. Changing the published lys binary for this is accepted; the release that carries it is a separate, deliberate act after docs/design/identity/IDENTITY-EVENTS.md's envelope version is ratified and recorded, never before, because publishing a crate that exposes a format freezes it (CLAUDE.md:78-80). Rejected: a verifier inside the directory service, which would be checking the service with the service and defeats the point of an independent audit.
decisions.quote: A verifier that needs the running directory service would be checking the service with the service, which defeats the point of an independent audit.
consequences: DIRECTORY-007 R3 adds the subcommand under the published discipline of lys log verify: one refusal class for every cryptographic or structural failure, pre-crypto refusals named on their own.
The verifier's row lands on main behind a check that the ratified envelope version is on main; landing on main publishes nothing.
The receipt's signed encoding stays with IDENTITY-EVENTS.md under DIRECTORY-003's joint review; the verifier is written against that document's version field and freezes no wire format.

decisions.title: A development install emits test receipts under a test key and a test tag, and a real key never verifies one
decisions.decided_by: Waffles, the lead, at 22:56 on 26 September 2026 (W3); recorded with DIRECTORY-007
decisions.context: Emitting any receipt outside a test is one of the three acts reserved for Tom (docs/design/lys-anchor/DECISIONS.md:333-335). A development install signs outside a cargo test harness, so its receipts had to be read either as that reserved act or as test receipts; read as the act, the whole path could never be proved end to end before Tom's release.
decisions.decision: A development install emits test receipts, signed with a test key and carrying a test tag, inside IDENTITY-001's development isolation, and never performs the reserved act. The verifier refuses a test-tagged receipt by name unless it is given the test key explicitly, and a real key never verifies a test receipt, so a test receipt never passes as real. Harness tests stay as well. Rejected: a development install that emits no receipts, and reading its receipts as the reserved act.
decisions.quote: A development install emits test receipts, signed with a test key and carrying a test tag, inside IDENTITY-001's development isolation, and never performs the act DECISIONS.md:335 reserves for Tom.
consequences: The test tag is the one field added to IDENTITY-001's receipt contract, under this ruling; IDENTITY-EVENTS.md carries it in the envelope.

lys log verify receipt takes --test-key beside --verifier-key: a test-tagged receipt is verified only against the test key and refused pre-crypto without it, saying to supply the test key; an untagged receipt is verified only against the verifier key.

DIRECTORY-007 R5 proves the whole path on the development install with test receipts and records the three outcomes: verified as a test receipt, refused for want of the test key, refused under another key.

decisions.title: An identity's lifecycle state is folded from its signed transition records and never set directly
decisions.decided_by: The lifecycle card's words, requested by tom; recorded with DIRECTORY-009
decisions.context: ADR-011 makes register, activate, suspend, reinstate and retire the only transitions, each one signed audit record, and DIRECTORY-003 R5 records the state beside each identity with its projection equal to replay. Nothing on main said whether the state is a value an API, a migration or a repair may write, which would leave two sources of truth: the stored state and the records that should explain it (principle P4 forbids a change followed by a best-effort log).
decisions.decision: The state at any moment is the fold of the identity's transition records in log order, from registered. No API, migration or repair sets a state; a transition validates against the folded state and the cause rule, appends its record through the directory's event path, and the state is read again by folding. A read answers the fold or refuses by name at the coordinate of a record the transition table refuses, and never answers a state past it, repairs the log or skips the record. Rejected: a stored state column set at transition and audited after it; a repair path that writes a state; and treating provisioned as a fifth state rather than a view over the facts beside the state.
decisions.quote: the state at any moment is folded from the log and never set directly
consequences: DIRECTORY-009 R3 builds the fold with a state type of exactly four values, and the state field DIRECTORY-003 R5's projection keeps is filled from the fold and from nothing else.

Retirement closes the identity and never its record: a retired identity's state, transitions and the record that put it there are read exactly as a live one's, and no row deletes or hides a record (L2, CN21).
A record the table refuses is a refusal named at its coordinate, answered by verifying the leaf against its receipt and reading the log by hand; the log is never repaired.
Every check that reads state reads the fold, so a suspended or retired identity fails by state alone whatever grants it holds.

decisions.title: A suspension takes effect at the next check, a session refresh is a check, and no Rauthy session is revoked at once
decisions.decided_by: The lead's answer L1 to the lifecycle card, from the lifecycle document on main; recorded with DIRECTORY-009
decisions.context: The lifecycle card asked whether a Rauthy session that outlives a suspension is revoked at once or at its next refresh. The lifecycle document says suspend and revoke both take effect at the next check and neither promises to roll back an action already admitted, and that a suspended identity's running executions stop at their next admission (docs/design/identity/LIFECYCLE-STATES-2026-09-22.md:51-53 and docs/design/identity/LIFECYCLE-STATES-2026-09-22.md:23); the directory design keeps open whether suspending a person also ends their sign-in session at Rauthy (its non-goals).
decisions.decision: A suspension or retirement takes effect at the next check and not before. The directory's resolution of a Rauthy-authenticated session at sign-in and at refresh is a check, so a session that outlives a suspension is refused at its next refresh and at every access check before that, by state, whatever grants it holds. Nothing in DIRECTORY-009 calls Rauthy to revoke, end or invalidate a session, keeps a list of sessions to end, or rolls back an admitted action. An at-once revocation of the Rauthy session would be a later revision of the suspend transition, and whether suspending also ends the sign-in session at Rauthy stays open as the design records it. Rejected: revoking the session at Rauthy at once within this brief, and treating a refresh as something other than a check.
decisions.quote: A refresh is a check, so a Rauthy session that outlives the suspension is refused at its next refresh and at every access check before that, by state, whatever grants it holds
consequences: DIRECTORY-009 R4 answers the access check state first and R5 refuses a suspended or retired identity at sign-in and at refresh by name, with the grant answerer called zero times.
The directory design gains constraint CN20 and a non-goal for the at-once revocation, so the later revision is a deliberate act and not a drift.
DIRECTORY-007 R4's step-1 leg that a suspended identity's sign-in is not refused on state is superseded when DIRECTORY-009 R5 lands, and the brief that lands second reconciles it under CN9.
An action admitted before a suspension stands; the record of the suspension is the only thing appended.

decisions.title: What a compaction could not keep is a lys.loss custom entry of ids, counts and SHA-256s
decisions.context: A Claude Code compaction replaces the model's context with a summary while the originals stay in the file. The home imports the compaction as Pi's compaction entry, which says where the kept range begins but never what fell outside it, so nothing in a home says what a compaction could not keep and nothing proves on a compacted session that the original is still there. Pi's grammar is adopted unchanged (P2), so any account has to be a lys custom entry, and a durable entry shape in the home is decided before homes carry it, as lys.given's was (ADR-013).
decisions.decision: Each compaction the importer writes is followed directly by one lys.loss custom entry, a side leaf whose parent is the compaction entry, whose data names the compaction by entry id, the first and last entry id of the span it summarised (the root-to-first-kept path entries, from the root or the previous compaction to the entry before the first kept one), the counts of that span's entries, messages, tool calls, tool results and blocks, its line bytes and block bytes counted separately, the counts of side-leaf and sidechain entries hanging from it by number only, the tokensBefore the harness reported (null when it reported none), a logicalParentUuid that names no record as unresolved, the SHA-256 of the span's first source line, of its last and of its lines concatenated in file order, the hash of the summary record's block and the span's distinct block hashes. Its keys are: compaction_id, first_kept (null when nothing is kept), span_first, span_last, entries, messages, tool_calls, tool_results, blocks, line_bytes, block_bytes, side_leaf_entries, sidechain_entries, tokens_before, unresolved_logical_parent, first_line_sha256, last_line_sha256, span_sha256, summary_record, block_hashes. Rejected: adding fields to Pi's compaction entry (it breaks CN4 and P2); hashing or listing side leaves and sidechain entries by id (their ids are drawn fresh on every import, so two imports of one file would disagree); and carrying any content, the summary included (P7).
consequences: HOME-010 adds the field to LanternData, the light act, its report and recall's rows, switches the fork to the typed field, and documents lit_in in docs/design/home/RECORD.md.
ADR-014's lantern shape is extended by one optional key, not replaced: a lantern lit before HOME-010 is read as it is and stays forkable.
ADR-017's older-record rule stays in force for a lantern with no lit_in; retiring it is a separate decision.

The fork's fixtures light with the light act every lantern it can produce, and write by hand only the records it cannot: a lantern with no lit_in, a copy whose lit_in names another session, and a malformed lit_in.
Once lanterns are lit under it in a real home the shape is frozen; a change to lit_in's meaning is a new version alongside.
RECORD.md states the rule, the exemption, the link-position rule and the unresolved marker.
Existing records are not rewritten; they compare by canonicalisation at check time.
A canonicalisation failure other than a path not existing is refused by path and operation.
The chain and the slug may see different forms of one working directory until the slug rule's own requirement settles it.
The loss entry is off the chain: context_path finds the compaction on the path unchanged and the render never writes the loss entry.
Two imports of one Claude Code file give loss entries equal byte for byte once the entry id, parentId, timestamp and data.compaction_id are masked.
The listing reads a span through the index and checks each named block by hash; a compaction with no loss entry, or pointing at itself, is reported unaccounted by entry id and never rewritten.
The shape is versioned by its custom type: a change is a new custom type alongside, never a mutation of lys.loss.

decisions.title: A Claude Code compaction imports as one Pi compaction at the summary record's place, keeping what Claude Code kept, and renders as the compact_boundary pair
decisions.decided_by: The home card lead's answers to the compaction survey; recorded with HOME-008
decisions.context: The importer handled only a legacy summary record, pointing the compaction at itself with tokensBefore 0; it read neither compact_boundary nor isCompactSummary, so a current compaction imported as a system harness event and a plain user message, and the render wrote a legacy summary line that the current Claude Code does not write. Measured on the survey's sample of 28 boundaries, anchorUuid named the summary record itself in 28 and all 94 preserved uuids sat before the boundary, so bounding the kept range by anchorUuid would count what Claude Code kept as lost and drop recent turns from the context path.
decisions.decision: A compact_boundary record imports as today, a lys.harness_event on the chain; the isCompactSummary record under it becomes one Pi compaction entry that takes that record's uuid, sits where the record sat as the child of the boundary's entry, carries the record's text as its summary and tokensBefore from compactMetadata.preTokens, and keeps the record only as a block; it is not a message entry. Its first kept entry is the earliest in file order of compactMetadata.preservedMessages.uuids when that list is non-empty, otherwise the first record whose parent is the summary record, and when there is none nothing is kept and firstKeptEntryId is the empty string, which keeps Pi's string type and is the only value that names no entry, so a compaction never names itself; anchorUuid is not used. A compact_boundary with no isCompactSummary record under it is not a compaction the harness completed: it stays a lys.harness_event, no summary is invented, and the listing reports it as a boundary without a summary. A legacy summary record keeps the entry its leafUuid names. A first kept entry not on record is refused by uuid. A logicalParentUuid naming no record is not refused. The Claude Code render writes a compaction as a compact_boundary record followed by an isCompactSummary user record holding the summary, then the kept entries, never the legacy summary line and never a custom entry. Rejected: bounding the kept range by anchorUuid; keeping the summary record as a message entry beside the compaction (the summary would be read twice); placing the compaction off the chain or re-parenting the next message (HOME-001 R3's parent-equals-source acceptance stands with no exception); and rendering the legacy summary line, which the current Claude Code does not write.
consequences: resolve_given lists appended_instructions and mcp_config ahead of user_claude_md, and the lys.given data shape of ADR-013 is unchanged.

RECORD.md states the one rule and names the old order as superseded by the commit that lands HOME-011 and its date; a reader tells an entry's order by comparing its recorded time with that date, and never by its harness_version.
A later harness card records its documents in the order its harness's request gives, and a harness-side input the request carries no trace of takes its place from the read order until it is measured.
A card that measures a real MCP server's tools position fixes mcp_config's place by that measurement.
HOME-001 R3's self-pointing summary mapping is replaced; the round-trip test that every message entry's parent equals its source parentUuid stands unchanged.
A home imported before this mapping is reported unaccounted by the listing; the act it names is re-importing the source file into a new home.

The rendered compact_boundary record's uuid is derived under render-uuid/v2, a new version alongside ADR-016's v1 that carries v1's derivation of the role record byte for byte and adds the role compact_boundary; v1's closed role list is not amended, a render with no compaction stays v1, and the render report names the version used.
The resume of the rendered pair is a per-version measurement (P6), recorded in PROOF-COMPACTION.md on Claude Code 2.1.283.
A boundary with no summary under it is counted by the listing by entry id, never turned into a compaction.

decisions.title: An admission policy judges at an instant its caller names; the live path names the present
decisions.decided_by: The card's words and the lys lead's answer on admit_at's parameters; recorded with LYSANCHOR-001
decisions.context: RecognisedCertificate could judge a certificate only at the present, because its admit called lys-core's verify_certificate_chain, which reads the clock itself. Its expiry test therefore slept 2.1 seconds, a wait the suite paid on every run and one whose outcome depends on a host's load. lys-core already exports verify_certificate_chain_at, frozen at 0.2.0, which takes the instant to judge against.
decisions.decision: RecognisedCertificate gains an inherent admit_at taking the submission, the SubmitterContext and the instant, built on verify_certificate_chain_at; AdmissionPolicy::admit keeps its signature and calls admit_at with the present, so a live request is judged exactly as before, and tests state the instants they judge at. Rejected: keeping the sleep; raising a timeout or splitting the test; injecting a clock into the policy instead of passing an instant; changing the AdmissionPolicy trait; and an admit_at taking only the asserted credential bytes, which would have to collapse the context's provenance before the call and could not represent the unidentified or transport-authenticated arms.
decisions.quote: The rule to meet: an admission policy judges at an instant its caller names.
consequences: The AdmissionPolicy trait, NotAdmitted and anchor/append.rs are unchanged; DP9 and DP23 in docs/design/lys-anchor/DECISIONS.md stand.
A test of the certificate gate's validity window states its instants and never sleeps.
lys-anchor depends on chrono through the workspace's existing entry.
verify_certificate_chain_at is used as lys-core 0.2.0 publishes it; lys-core is not changed.

decisions.title: A certificate is self-signed when its subject key is the issuer key and its signature verifies under it, never by its names
decisions.decided_by: The lead for lys, answering the lys-core self-signed survey; recorded with LYSCORE-001
decisions.context: verify_certificate_chain_at refused a certificate when its raw subject and issuer DN bytes were equal. The authority writes its issuer DN as the lowercase hex of its public key, so a certificate it legitimately issued to a subject named with that string was refused although its signature verified. A certificate whose subject key was the issuer's own key, issued over a request made with the authority's key, carried different names and verified. C23 ('Self-signed certificates are rejected') had been ticked on the name comparison.
decisions.decision: Self-signed is judged by keys: a certificate is self-signed when its subject public key is the supplied issuer key, compared as decoded Ed25519 points, and its signature verifies under that key with verify_strict, and such a certificate is refused whatever its names. A certificate issued to a subject whose name equals the issuer's hex-key common name is judged on its real issuer and verifies. Rejected: keeping the DN-byte comparison as a heuristic screen; keeping truly self-signed certificates with differing names verifying.
consequences: lys ca verify and lys verify --cert exit 0 for a hex-common-name certificate the issuer signed, and exit 1 for a certificate self-signed by keys.
C23 is restated with the key-based definition and ticks again only on review.
A certificate issued by issue_certificate_for_request over a request made with the authority's own key is refused; CHANGELOG records it.
DIRECTORY-013's fold records certificate_chain_invalid for a leaf self-signed by keys and issues a legitimately issued hex-common-name leaf.

decisions.title: The self-signed fix and the verify_certificate_chain caveat land on main with no lys-core release, after DIRECTORY-013
decisions.decided_by: The lead for lys, answering the lys-core self-signed survey; recorded with LYSCORE-001
decisions.context: The revocation brief's first round ruled the rustdoc caveat on verify_certificate_chain a documentation-only lys-core release of its own. Main carries unreleased lys-core commits including the unpublished lys/delegation/v1, which publishing would freeze before its ordering fold exists, there is no v0.2.0 tag to branch from, and a release carrying the self-signed fix is not documentation-only. DIRECTORY-013's draft forbids changing verify_certificate_chain(_at) and their documentation, and its fold calls verify_certificate_chain_at.
decisions.decision: This card lands the key-based self-signed rule and the rustdoc caveat on main and cuts no crates.io release; a release is its own act after the ordering fold. DIRECTORY-013 lands first and is not amended; this card's build is blocked until DIRECTORY-013's roadmap row reads landed on origin/main. Rejected: a documentation-only release cut from main or from a 0.2.0 base in this card; landing this card first and amending DIRECTORY-013.
consequences: No lys-core version bump or publish in LYSCORE-001; the change waits under CHANGELOG's Unreleased section.
LYSCORE-001 carries DIRECTORY-013 in depends_on and a blocked_by command that reads its roadmap row on origin/main.
LYSCORE-001 adds a fold test to DIRECTORY-013's revocation_fold.rs and edits nothing else of that card.

decisions.title: The given statement is a lys/attestation/v2 over the RFC 8785 bytes of lys.given's data, written only when render-launch is given a key
decisions.decided_by: The lead's rulings on the given-statement card; the canonical form chosen by HOME-008's author and proposed with that brief
decisions.context: CONFORMANCE row 6.5 asks that what an agent was given be a signed statement checked with lys verify --attestation. The lys.given entry records the hashes of the documents a session was given and no hash of itself, lys-core's attestation signs SHA-256 of a payload, and a signed form is frozen from its first signature, so the bytes signed have to be named so a stranger can rebuild them with standard tooling.
decisions.decision: The given statement is lys-core's existing lys/attestation/v2 over the RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme) bytes of the lys.given entry's data, so its signed payload hash is the given hash render-launch reports as given_sha256. It is written only when render-launch is given a key: kept as a block named by a lys.given_statement entry hung under the lys.given entry, and as given-statement.cose and given-data.json under --out for lys verify. Rejected: serialising the record in struct field order, which a stranger cannot rebuild without the Rust type; signing the 64-hex hash string, whose attested hash would be SHA-256 of the hex and not the given hash; adding the given hash to the template_render event, which HOME-003 keeps unaltered; and changing lys verify's one failure message to name the file, which would change the published lys for every user.
consequences: A new underscore-prefixed binding under crates/ fails the ast-grep leg with the rule's reason.
A guard is named and dropped by name; a value with no use is not bound; the bare `_` stays available.
The rule is a candidate for Cambium to adopt in its own gated change.
The RFC 8785 form of lys.given's data is a wire contract from the first signature; changing it means a new statement type alongside, never a mutation.
A render with no key writes the lys.given entry as HOME-003 records it and no statement, and says unsigned.
The statement is checked with the unchanged lys verify; which key signed is checked by comparing its signer public key with an expected key until row 6.1's --cert checks it against a certificate.
The start statement and the role-move statement are later statements over the START launch record and the ROLES version record, written when those records land.

decisions.title: A trait parameter one implementation ignores is a bare `_` where the trait cannot drop it
decisions.decided_by: The lead for the identity line, answering this card's survey; recorded with LYSCORE-002
decisions.context: The words give an unused trait parameter two ways out: use it, or change the trait so it is not asked for. AdmissionPolicy::admit needs both of its parameters across its implementations, and LeafStore is in the published lys-log-store 0.2.0, where changing it breaks consumers. Neither way out is open without changing behaviour or API.
decisions.decision: An implementation that has no use for a parameter which another implementation of the same trait needs, or which a published trait asks for, writes the bare `_` pattern. The bare `_` binds nothing, so it is the words' 'not bound at all', and it is not the underscore-prefixed name the rule refuses. The trait is not changed. Rejected: changing AdmissionPolicy or LeafStore, adding a use to a parameter the implementation does not need, and keeping an underscore-prefixed name.
consequences: AcceptAll, MaxSize and the certificate policy under AdmissionPolicy, and the LyingStore, DecliningSigner and RecordPolicy test fakes, write their ignored parameters as a bare `_`.
The AdmissionPolicy, LeafStore, Signer and AnchorTask declarations do not change.
The rule admits a bare `_` and refuses an underscore-prefixed name, and one acceptance line shows both.

decisions.title: Cambium's ast-grep rules are carried into lys only where they can fire
decisions.decided_by: Archie, lead for lys, in rulings to the lys-gate card's runs; recorded with LYSCORE-001
decisions.context: The words asked for the same rule set Cambium carries. Three of Cambium's six rules concern async code and door handlers, and lys has no async fn, no tokio and no std Mutex; Cambium carries no _name rule.
decisions.decision: lys carries mod-rs-declarations-only, no-let-underscore-on-results and no-lint-bypass-attributes, and records no-std-mutex-in-async, no-timer-in-door-handlers and no-timer-import-in-door-handlers as not carried with the finding that they cannot fire; the _name rule is its own card. Rejected: copying all six rules, which would look like cover the scan cannot give.
consequences: A session, canon or fork child holding an entry the render cannot shape no longer renders; the refusal names the entry to repair and nothing is written.

Sessions the importer wrote with a redacted_thinking part that carried no data hold thinkingSignature null and now refuse to render; the importer's own defaults are the other half of the defect and belong to the importer card, not to the render.
A session holding an error or an aborted turn does not render until the Claude Code format has a value for it.
The bytes rendered from a session that carries every field do not change, so every pinned render hash stands.
The card that lands lys's first async code carries no-std-mutex-in-async and names this decision in its brief.
The lys and Cambium rule sets differ, and neither is edited to match the other.
A _name rule for lys is written by a card of its own that handles each binding by its act.

decisions.title: Needs a new person is a view worked out on read from an agent's registration and its person's retire record, never stored or appended
decisions.decided_by: The lead for the identity line, answering the survey of the lifecycle conformance card; recorded with DIRECTORY-019 (RM-032)
decisions.context: CONFORMANCE row 3.1 flags an agent whose person is retired as needing a new person. The lifecycle-hand brief DIRECTORY-009 (RM-017) says no policy causes a transition and that the only automatic effect a suspension or retirement has on other identities is the grant check, and ADR-011 keeps an agent's responsible person for life. A flag appended as a signed record on each agent, or one that moved the agent's state, would contradict both.
decisions.decision: An agent's needs-a-new-person flag is worked out each time its lifecycle record is read, from the responsible person its registration names and that person's retire record: it is true when that person's folded state is retired and false otherwise, a suspended person included. Nothing is appended to any agent's history, no transition is made on the agent, the agent keeps its own state, and no responsible person changes. The flag records a fact, that the agent's person is retired; clearing it needs the reassignment card, which is the one that revises ADR-011's responsible person for life. Rejected: a signed flag record appended on each agent when its person is retired; moving the agent to another state with its person.
consequences: Each agent's history stays as it is, and the lifecycle-hand brief's rule that retiring someone has no automatic effect on other identities except the grant check holds.
The agent's own state is unchanged by its person's retirement, and its derived grants refuse at the check as they already do.
ADR-011 and DIRECTORY-003 R1 are not revised: the responsible person stays for life until the reassignment card revises that rule.
A suspended person's agents are not flagged; what a suspension stops stays open.

decisions.title: lys recognises test code by structure the file carries, for ast-grep and clippy alike
decisions.decided_by: Archie, lead for lys, in rulings to the lys-gate card's runs; recorded with LYSCORE-001
decisions.context: An unwrap/expect/panic rule needs to tell test code from library code. 227 calls sat outside #[test] fns and #[cfg(test)] mods, in 2 fixtures and 47 sibling *_tests.rs files, and 106 files opted out of clippy with a per-module #![allow], which the new no-lint-bypass-attributes rule reports.
decisions.decision: Test code is a file whose first line is #![cfg(test)], a #[cfg(test)] mod body, a #[test] fn body, or a path under a crate's tests/ directory; every file only ever compiled as a test carries the first-line marker, and clippy.toml's allow-unwrap-in-tests, allow-expect-in-tests and allow-panic-in-tests replace the per-module #![allow]. Rejected: an exemption list of file names in the rule, and rewriting the test helpers' calls.
consequences: Every new fixture, sibling test file, integration root or test harness module begins with #![cfg(test)].
No rule or config holds a list of file names to exempt.
CLAUDE.md and Cargo.toml name clippy.toml in place of the per-module #![allow]; lys's clippy.toml takes the opposite setting from Cambium's.
No #[allow] of any kind replaces a removed one.

decisions.title: Permission enforcement through SpiceDB on the standalone identity server enters the directory design, on a decided grant representation
decisions.decided_by: The owning lead's answers to the directory road-step-2 survey and drafts, the grant representation with Apollo as second reader and the freshness mechanism as built with a second reader; recorded with DIRECTORY-025
decisions.context: The directory design lists 'Road step 2 onward: capability certificates, arbitrary grants and their enforcement, ...' as a non-goal, and CN11 gives live capability policy and its enforcement to step 2, while step 1 installs SpiceDB and asks it nothing (DIRECTORY-002 R4). Step 2 is defined in docs/design/identity/STATEMENT-2026-09-22.md (The road, line 143) as the door asking SpiceDB on every call. The road-step-2 card asks for step 2 of the directory design for the identity server, so without a ruling a reader of DESIGN.md would find the brief contradicting the design's own scope.
decisions.decision: Amend the design narrowly: permission enforcement through SpiceDB on the standalone identity server leaves the 'Road step 2 onward' non-goal and becomes a goal of the directory design, and CN11 gains one appended ruling line saying so. Everything else in the non-goal stays, and neither the non-goal's text nor CN11's is reworded; the non-goal's reason gains one appended sentence saying it does not cover that enforcement. The grant representation (C5) is a technical decision of the owning lead with a second reader, not one left open for Tom, and is decided here: every grant, root or delegated, is its own grant object in SpiceDB, keyed by its grant identifier, and is exactly 3 relationships: the resource's relationship to the grant object under the grant's action; the grant's holder relationship to the identity that holds it, carrying an expiry caveat that ends no later than its source's; and the grant's standing relationship, which for a delegated grant is its source relationship to its source grant, the source relation the permission walks, and for a root grant, which has no source, is its root relationship, the grant object's relationship to the directory's root authority, one object per directory and the same object the issue_root permission is checked against when a person issues a root grant through POST /grants/roots; a permission holds through a grant only while the grant's standing holds, a root grant's through its root relationship and a delegated grant's through its source grant's standing, so derivation is a walk of the source relation that ends at the directory's root authority in a bounded number of steps, a grant that stands on neither a source relationship nor a root relationship is malformed and refused, and deleting a grant's standing relationship refuses its holder and every grant derived from it at once; two live grants giving the same holder the same action on the same resource are two grant objects, each with its own relationships, and revoking one leaves the other standing; withdrawing a grant deletes its relationships and those of every grant derived from it through the source relation on the same committed revoke event, the withdrawn grant's standing relationship alone in the first write and the rest in further writes within SpiceDB's configured max_updates_per_write. The expiry bound is refused, never clamped: a delegation asking for an expiry later than its source grant's is refused by name before anything is committed, and a committed delegation event that nonetheless asks for one is refused by the projector by name, which writes no relationship for it and stops there; a silent clamp would make the record say one thing and the grant another. Rejected: sitting beside the non-goal as a named exception, which leaves the design's stated scope contradicting the brief; rewording the non-goal or CN11; and bringing Cambium's door into this cluster.
consequences: CN11 gains one appended line naming ADR-078, and the 'Road step 2 onward' non-goal's reason gains one appended sentence saying permission enforcement through SpiceDB on the standalone identity server is not covered by it; the non-goal's text and every other sentence of the design are unchanged.
DIRECTORY-002 R4's step-1 sentence stays word for word in deploy/identity/README.md, which gains one step-2 sentence beside it; nothing in crates/lys/src/identity/ checks SpiceDB or writes to it.

Every grant and permission check the identity server makes asks SpiceDB; the administrator's admission by configured issuer and subject (P9, C13) is the one named exception and never asks SpiceDB, because it is how an operator bootstraps the directory before any relation exists.
The reverse question of DIRECTORY-006 R5, who can act on a resource, is answered by SpiceDB's LookupSubjects at the same revision as the forward CheckPermission.
Cambium's door asking SpiceDB on every call is a later Cambium card; an agent calling through the door is not refused by the identity server's enforcement until that card lands.

The grant representation (C5) is decided as above and the grant-representation non-goal's reason gains one appended ruling line saying so, its text unchanged; after a root grant is withdrawn no relationship of it or of any grant derived from it remains.

This ruling, together with DIRECTORY-006 R1 to R5 as built and accepted on hand/DIRECTORY-006-R5 at e525a91 after a second reader's review, stands as the ratification DIRECTORY-006 R1 and DIRECTORY-006's blocked_by ask for; no separate contract review is waited on. The grant-representation non-goal stays recorded as open for Tom, and a later ruling by Tom amends the contract.

A person's root authority on a resource comes from a root grant the directory's root authority, one person fixed when the grants are opened, issues through DIRECTORY-006's root issue; a root grant has no source, its expiry is the end its issuer states or no end, and every delegated grant ends no later than its source. No other bootstrap is added.

The freshness mechanism (C25) is settled by the owning lead with a second reader as DIRECTORY-006 R4 builds it: a check is answered only from a projection that has applied every committed revocation it depends on, and otherwise it is refused with StaleDecision, the refusal DIRECTORY-006 builds for a stale projection, to which DIRECTORY-025 R4 adds the affected grant's identifier, while unrelated authority stays usable. Suspension semantics stay open and ADR-011 stays proposed.

decisions.title: A Claude Code import builds its session under a staging name and publishes it once
decisions.decided_by: The home line's lead, answering the survey of the repeated-work card; recorded with HOME-020
decisions.context: Every imported entry went through Session::append_entry, which syncs the line, syncs the index row and writes the head through a temporary file, a rename and a directory sync: about five syncs per record, though the import sets the head once at its end. Appending in place with no sync until the end cannot be repaired by the existing reconcile: a crash can leave a torn or zero-filled last line that Index::scan refuses as Malformed, so the session will not open, a head still at the header, and a re-import refused as Exists; and the original bytes are never rewritten (P1), so a torn tail cannot be trimmed.
decisions.decision: The import command builds its new session under the staging name `<id>.jsonl.importing` beside `sessions/<id>.jsonl`, holding `<id>.lock` throughout: the header and every entry line are written to the staging file with no sync, and the index rows and the head are kept in memory. It then publishes once, in this order: one sync of the staging file; the index written whole to `<id>.index.jsonl` through a temporary file, synced and renamed; the head written once to `<id>.head` through a temporary file, synced and renamed; one sync of the sessions directory; the staging file renamed to `<id>.jsonl`; one more sync of the sessions directory. A crash before the rename leaves no session under the final name, so a re-import is not refused as Exists; the next import of that id and the next open of that session file, each holding the lock, remove the staging file and, when `<id>.jsonl` is absent, the `<id>.index.jsonl` and `<id>.head` a part-way publish left. Rejected: appending in place and leaving a session that refuses by name after a crash; extending reconcile to trim an unsynced tail.
consequences: docs/design/directory/design.json gains a goal for the certificate half of step 2, the 'Road step 2 onward' non-goal no longer lists it, and CN11 and CN1 each end with one ruling line citing this decision.

The rest of step 2 (SpiceDB as a service, the door asking it on every call, per-execution credentials, presenting the certificate at spawn) stays a non-goal of this cluster and belongs to its own cards.
A brief that lands after DIRECTORY-031 and needs the CN1 ruling cites it rather than writing a second line.
docs/design/home/RECORD.md states the staged import's rule beside the per-append durability order, which is unchanged for every other append.

Only an import into a session it creates is staged; import_claude_code given a session that is already open keeps append_entry's per-entry syncs, since a rename cannot publish a session that already exists.
Reconcile is not extended and no session file is trimmed, rewritten or truncated; recovering a session whose last line a crash tore is its own decision.
A staging file does not end in `.jsonl`, so Home::session_ids never lists it as a session.
The block store's two syncs per new block are unchanged and are not part of the import's bounded count; they are counted beside it.

decisions.title: An agent certificate's validity window comes from the directory's configuration: 30 days by default, 90 days at most
decisions.decided_by: Archie, lead for the identity line, ruling on the capability-claim card; recorded with DIRECTORY-031
decisions.context: DIRECTORY-031 issues an enduring agent a certificate whose notBefore and notAfter govern its life; its typed claim carries no validity window of its own, and its verifier refuses the certificate past its notAfter through lys-core's certificate-expired check. The draft let the operator set the lifetime on every issuance call, with no default and no upper bound, so one typo could issue a certificate that outlives the grants it lists and the person's role behind it; revocation (the DP26 fold) is not built yet, so expiry is the only thing that bounds a certificate today.
decisions.decision: The directory's configuration holds a default validity window and a maximum, shipped as 30 days (2592000 seconds) and 90 days (7776000 seconds). An issuance call with no window takes the default; the operator may ask for a shorter window, never a longer one, and a request above the maximum is refused by name, lifetime_above_maximum, naming the maximum. The certificate records the window it was given as its own notBefore and notAfter. A verifier takes a set of trusted issuer keys, never exactly one, and the certificate names the issuer key that signed it in X.509's Authority Key Identifier by its issuer-key fingerprint, the first 20 bytes of the SHA-256 of that key's SubjectPublicKeyInfo (RFC 7093 method 1, matching the SubjectKeyIdentifier of lys-core's issuer certificate), so a later rotation of the issuer key needs no change of format. Rejected: an operator-supplied lifetime with no default and no bound, which lets a typo outlive a withdrawn grant; a window fixed in code with no configuration; and a verifier bound to exactly one issuer key, which would make every rotation a format change.
decisions.quote: A value the directory's configuration states. The configuration holds a default validity window and a maximum, with 30 days and 90 days as the shipped values. The operator may ask for a shorter window on an issuance call, and never a longer one. A request above the maximum is refused by name, naming the maximum, and a request with no window takes the default. The certificate records the window it was given.
consequences: DIRECTORY-031 R6 reads the default and the maximum from the directory service's configuration and refuses a longer window with lifetime_above_maximum; its acceptance covers a default issuance, a shorter request and a longer request refused by name.

A short window bounds how long a certificate outlives a withdrawn grant until the DP26 fold of the revocation card is built, and the maximum keeps an operator's typo from issuing a certificate that outlives its person's role.

verify_agent_capability takes a set of trusted issuer keys and compares the certificate's Authority Key Identifier with the signing key's fingerprint, so the issuer key rotation card changes configuration, not the format of lys/agent-capability/v1.

decisions.title: A session credential is a random value the directory issues when the agent's signed report-back over a directory-issued challenge creates the session, and keeps only as a hash
decisions.decided_by: Archie, lead for the identity line, answering the session card's rounds; recorded with DIRECTORY-026
decisions.context: Road step 2 keeps the enduring agent and each session's credential apart (docs/design/identity/STATEMENT-2026-09-22.md:166). The provision card's contract left what a session credential is open for the session card, naming three readings: a per-session lys certificate, a lys/delegation/v1 SpeaksFor delegation, and an ADR-001 handle. The product never runs an agent (ADR-007), so the directory never sees a start directly, and a crashed agent never reports its end. The start card ties a running agent to the command it was given through a launch record id. A new signed tag freezes the first time anything signs under it.
decisions.decision: The session credential is 32 random bytes the directory issues when the session is created. The directory keeps only their SHA-256, on the session record, and returns the value once, in the answer to the report-back that created the session; the session presents the value to the directory, which is the only party that checks it. A session is created when the started agent first reports back and proves it is the agent with its enrolled key, and only for an agent whose certificate has been issued. Before reporting back, the agent asks the directory for a challenge: 32 random bytes the directory issues once, for that agent and a launch record id the agent supplies, kept until used or until it expires more than 60 seconds after issue. The proof is an Ed25519 signature under the tag lys/session-start/v1 (ADR-080). The directory verifies the signature before anything else: an unsigned or badly signed proof, or one naming an agent it does not hold or one with no enrolled key, is refused proof_invalid with one body and touches no challenge, and only a correctly signed proof receives the state-revealing refusals. It admits the proof only when the challenge is one it issued to that agent, unused and unexpired, the directory named is itself and the launch record id matches the challenge's, and it marks the challenge used in the same act that creates the session. Two acts end a session: the agent reporting its end with its credential, and the directory's administrator stopping it. Ending changes the record's state, so the credential is refused at once, naming the ended session. Rejected: a per-session lys certificate, because nobody verifies a session credential offline in this card, so a signed artifact buys nothing and would freeze a format before anything needs it; a lys/delegation/v1 SpeaksFor delegation, framed for an offline root key and a seat subject, whose module says not to invent a consumer; an ADR-001 handle, which waits on the unbuilt secrets broker (SECRETS-002); creating the session when a start command is rendered; and expiry of a session.
decisions.quote: None of the three. The session credential is a random value the directory issues when the session is created. The directory keeps only its hash, on the session record, and the session presents the value to the directory. The reason is that in this card the directory is the only party that checks a session credential. Nobody verifies it offline, so a signed artifact buys nothing here and would freeze a format before anything needs it. A handle waits on the unbuilt secrets broker (SECRETS-002). SpeaksFor is framed for an offline root key and a seat subject, and delegation/mod.rs says not to invent a consumer. Refusing is a change to the record's state, so ending a session refuses its credential at once. The brief records this choice and its reason as an ADR at the next free id, and names a signed session credential as later work, for when a party other than the directory must check a session.
consequences: The session credential is distinct from the agent's one certificate (ADR-008) and never replaces it. No session credential value appears in a start command, a launch record, an event, a log or a document; the session_started event carries only its SHA-256, which reveals nothing because the value is 32 random bytes.

P9 gives way narrowly: an agent authenticated by its enrolled key creates and ends its own session record, and nothing else. Every other mutation by a caller who is not an administrator is still refused in step 1 by name.
The launch record id is carried as supplied; the check that the launch record exists and belongs to the agent is the start card's, so the two cards do not depend on each other.

A session is refused to a retired agent and to an agent whose certificate has been revoked, the revocation read only through the certificate revocation card's fold, and no open session is ended by either. Suspension refuses nothing here while it stays open. Ending open sessions is the emergency-stop card's.
A crashed agent's session stays open until an operator stops it. Lapsing a stale session is its own card.
A signed session credential is later work, for when a party other than the directory must check a session. It is a new format with its own version and review, never a change to this one.
This decision supersedes, by closing it, the earlier draft of the same card (run d5055cc1) and the decision it held there, which never reached main.

decisions.title: lys/session-start/v1 signs five fields, the tag, the agent id, the directory's identifier, the launch record id and a directory-issued nonce, and is proposed in the wire-format register until ratified
decisions.context: The session card's report-back is a new signed statement, and a domain-separation tag freezes the first time anything signs under it (CLAUDE.md, wire formats are forever). docs/design/WIRE-FORMATS.md is the register every wire contract passes through, proposed, ratified, frozen, with ratification a recorded human decision in its decision log. The identity line's lead fixed the statement's content in the session card's rounds; the format itself is ratified in the register, not by this ledger.
decisions.decision: The report-back is an Ed25519 signature by the agent's enrolled key over the 20 ASCII bytes of lys/session-start/v1, one 0x00 byte, then the agent directory id, the directory's own identifier and the launch record id, each as its UTF-8 length in 4 bytes big-endian followed by its bytes, then the 32-byte nonce, a challenge the directory issued once to that agent for that launch record id and admits for 60 seconds after issue. Freshness (the nonce), audience (the directory's identifier) and the launch record id are in the first version because the tag cannot gain them after it freezes. The format is proposed in docs/design/WIRE-FORMATS.md's decision log; the tests sign under it with disposable test keys only, and no production agent signs under it until the register shows it ratified. Rejected: a four-field message without the directory's identifier, which could not say which directory a proof was made for; a message without the launch record id, which could not tie a session to the command it was started by; a signature over the fields without a directory-issued nonce, which a replay would satisfy; and treating this ledger entry as the ratification, which the register reserves to its own decision log.
decisions.quote: Five fields. The signed lys/session-start/v1 message carries the tag, the agent id, the directory's own identifier, the launch record id and the nonce. The later sentence adds the launch record id and removes nothing, and the acceptance line for a proof naming another directory stands.
consequences: The statement is reviewed adversarially before any code signs under it, and a change after it freezes is a new tag alongside, never a mutation.
The status moves to decided when docs/design/WIRE-FORMATS.md's decision log records the format ratified; until then no production agent signs under lys/session-start/v1.

The bytes are a tagged, length-prefixed preimage signed with plain Ed25519, not COSE_Sign1: the directory is the only verifier, as for lys/sealed-envelope/v1, which WIRE-FORMATS.md keeps out of COSE on the same ground.

decisions.title: Issuance enters the lys-log-store log `lys log` keeps before any certificate is written, and the issuer holds only the CA key
decisions.decided_by: Archie, lead for the identity line, answering the row 6.4 survey
decisions.context: CONFORMANCE row 6.4 asks that certificate issuance is entered in a transparency log and that anyone verifies the certificate and its inclusion offline with standard tools. The published `lys` crate (0.2.0) cannot depend on lys-anchor, which is publish = false, and docs/design/lys-anchor/BUILD-PLAN.md section 2.5 keeps anchor surface out of `lys`; row 6.4's brief column says 'on lys-log-store'. The lys/log-inclusion-proof/v1 artifact embeds a checkpoint signed with the log's key, so writing it at issuance would make the issuer hold that key too.
decisions.decision: `lys ca issue` enters every certificate it produces, on both issuance paths, in the lys-log-store log that `lys log` keeps, as one leaf whose bytes are the certificate's DER and nothing else, before any certificate file is written; if the log refuses the entry no certificate is written. The issuer holds only the CA key: issuance appends the leaf, writes the certificate and the leaf file, and reports the log and the leaf index, and the log's operator makes the lys/log-inclusion-proof/v1 artifact with `lys log prove inclusion`, which holds the log's key. Rejected: giving `lys` a dependency on lys-anchor, which would stop `lys` being publishable and reverse BUILD-PLAN section 2.5; putting issue-and-enter in the lys-anchor binary instead of `lys ca issue`; and requiring the issuer to hold the log's key to write the artifact at issuance. The issuer-only entry is the required path, and a production issuer never holds the log's key. `--log-key` and `--artifact-out` stay on `lys ca issue` only as an optional path for one operator who holds both keys, as tests and proofs with test keys do; given one without the other, issuance refuses.
consequences: `lys` keeps lys-core and lys-log-store as its only lys dependencies and stays publishable; lys-anchor and lys-anchor-cli stay publish = false.
No new wire format: the leaf is the DER alone and the artifact is the existing lys/log-inclusion-proof/v1; no draft format from unstable-anchor is reached by issuance.
The entry precedes every certificate write, so a refused entry leaves no certificate on disk.
Tests and proofs use test keys and a test log; production keys and the production log stay the project owner's acts under row 6.6.
Withdrawal (row 6.3) and typed claims (row 6.2) are not part of issuance-with-entry.
An issuance that writes the artifact itself happens only where one operator holds both the CA key and the log's key; the production issuer, holding only the CA key, never takes that path.

decisions.title: A holding with an end date moves at its next renewal by default; one without moves only by a deliberate act
decisions.context: Conformance row 4.6 (docs/design/identity/CONFORMANCE.md) is open: which policy is the default. ADR-006 says a holder moves by a deliberate recorded act or by an explicit rule shown in advance, such as a move at the next renewal, and that which of the two is the default is open. No brief on the main branch defines a renewal, so the roles brief introduces it as a recorded act. Written by Apollo as author with the roles brief DIRECTORY-021, with Archie as second reader. Recorded as proposed: it becomes decided only when Tom rules on it or signs the card off. It answers the sentence ADR-006 left open and cites ADR-006; it does not supersede it.
decisions.decision: A move at the next renewal is the default for a holding with an end date, shown on the holder as the date it will move, which is the holding's end date, with the words that its next renewal moves it to the current version and who can stop the move. A renewal, which the roles brief introduces, is a deliberate recorded act by the person the holder answers to (the responsible person of ADR-011) or by an owner of the role's project: a new grant of the holding with a new end date, recorded naming the actor, the holding it renews and the version it lands on. So the move rides on a deliberate recorded act and no holder ever moves without one; unrenewed, the holding lapses at its end date under ADR-006 and does not move. A holding with no end date has no renewal, so whatever the role's default it moves only by a deliberate act, and the screen says so on that holder. A role carries a default policy, and a newly made role's default is a move at the next renewal; a holding with an end date takes that default at grant time, and the person the holder answers to or an owner of the role's project may change the policy of one holding afterwards, recorded with who did it and in which capacity. The holding's own policy governs it. Under a move only by a deliberate act a renewal is made at the version the holding holds; under a move at the next renewal it is made at the role's current version. Changing a role's default applies to holdings granted after the change and moves nothing that exists. Rejected: holders staying on their version until moved as the default for a holding with an end date, because the renewal is a deliberate recorded act the move can ride on; and a policy set only per role, because one holding could not then be kept apart.
consequences: Each holding shows its policy; one with an end date under a move at the next renewal shows its end date as its move date, the words that its next renewal moves it to the current version, and who can stop the move.

The role screen shows the role's default and marks each holding with an end date whose policy differs from it; a holding with no end date is unmarked and shows only the words Moves only by a deliberate act.
Nothing renews a holding but the renewal act; a version change never extends an end date (ADR-006).

decisions.title: A role is a set of grant templates copied at grant time, not a live group
decisions.context: Conformance row 4.7 (docs/design/identity/CONFORMANCE.md) is open: role as live group or template copied at grant time. ADR-006's consequence says the same stays open, while ADR-006 itself forbids a holder changing version silently as a side effect of an edit. The roles card decides the row. Written by Apollo as author with the roles brief DIRECTORY-021, with Archie as second reader. Recorded as proposed: it becomes decided only when Tom rules on it or signs the card off. It answers the sentence ADR-006 left open and cites ADR-006; it does not supersede it.
decisions.decision: A role is a template copied at grant time, not a live group. A holding names the role and the version it holds, the grants it carries are made from that version's templates when the holding is granted, and an edit to the role changes none of them. Who holds a role remains answerable as a query over holdings. Only the versioned grant templates make a version; a title edit is recorded and makes no version, and conformance 4.1's job and profile stay proposed and outside. Rejected: a live group, whose membership carries the role's current grants, because a live group would change every holder's permissions at the moment of the edit, which ADR-006 forbids.
consequences: A holding records its role, its version and the ids of the grants copied into it; nothing links a granted holding's grants to later versions.
Editing a role's templates makes the next version and changes no holding, grant or end date.
Who holds a role, and on which version, is answered from the holdings, never from a member list kept on the role.

decisions.title: A named leaf in the file store is a whole, flushed leaf, and the no-replace link is its commit point
decisions.decided_by: The card's words and the lead's answers to its survey; recorded with LYSLOGSTORE-001
decisions.context: FileLeafStore created a leaf file under its final 20-digit name and then wrote it, so a crash or failed write left a torn leaf that the next open counted and Log::open's one-leaf-ahead repair pinned, and a failure after naming left the extent behind the disk so the store later refused its own leaf as another writer's. BACKENDS.md criterion 1 (durable on return) says nothing about what a named leaf is between a write's start and its return. DIRECTORY-003's uncertain append settles by reading a leaf back and needs a named leaf to mean a committed one.
decisions.decision: A file under a 20-digit leaf name is always a whole, flushed leaf; only dot-prefixed temporary files in leaves/ may be partial. A leaf is written and flushed in a hidden temporary file, then linked to its final name by an operation that refuses to replace, then the temporary name is removed and leaves/ is flushed. The successful link is the commit point: the extent advances past the leaf whatever happens next. A failed temporary-name removal still returns Ok; a failed leaves/ flush returns StoreError::LeafDurabilityUncertain carrying the index, and the handle refuses further appends with it until reopened. A writable open flushes leaves/ before counting and fails with Io when that flush fails; a read-only open (FileLeafStore::open_read_only) counts the named leaves without flushing; neither counts, deletes or changes a leftover temporary file. Rejected: naming the leaf first and writing into it (today's torn-leaf shape); deleting leftover temporary files at open, which would make a read-only open mutate the store; flushing at a read-only open, which would turn a status on read-only media into an error; and reporting a post-link failure as Io, which left the extent behind and made the next append report the store's own leaf as LeafAlreadyWritten.
consequences: StoreError gains LeafDurabilityUncertain, carrying the index and the failed flush's io error as its source (ADR-060 keeps LeafAlreadyWritten for another writer).
FileLeafStore::open performs a directory flush and fails with Io when it fails, and FileLeafStore::open_read_only never flushes; neither deletes or rewrites a file.
Leftover temporary files accumulate after crashes until a separate maintenance act, run only while holding the write lock, clears them.
The on-disk layout and the LeafStore trait's methods are unchanged; the invariant is local state, not a wire contract.
DIRECTORY-003 treats LeafDurabilityUncertain as uncertain and settles by reading the leaf back, and lands after LYSLOGSTORE-001.

decisions.title: LeafAlreadyWritten means another writer holds the index, and the store never reports its own leaf as another writer's
decisions.decided_by: The card's words and the lead's answers to its survey; recorded with LYSLOGSTORE-001
decisions.context: store.rs's contract says LeafAlreadyWritten is a conflict, not a resume signal: a refusal at N means another writer holds that position. FileLeafStore named a leaf before put_leaf returned, so a failure after naming left the extent behind the disk and the next put_leaf at that index was refused as LeafAlreadyWritten, the store reporting its own leaf as another writer's. A consumer settling an uncertain append (DIRECTORY-003) would then read a conflict where there was none.
decisions.decision: LeafAlreadyWritten is returned only when the index is behind the extent or the no-replace link finds the final name taken by an entry this call did not link. Once this call's link succeeds the extent advances past the leaf whatever happens next, so no later step of the same call and no later call on the same handle reports that leaf as LeafAlreadyWritten; a post-link failure that leaves durability in doubt is LeafDurabilityUncertain (ADR-059). Rejected: reporting a post-link failure as Io and leaving the extent behind, which made the next append report the store's own leaf as LeafAlreadyWritten; and treating LeafAlreadyWritten as a resume signal a caller may retry through.
consequences: LeafAlreadyWritten's documentation in error.rs and store.rs keeps meaning another writer only.
A handle that returned LeafDurabilityUncertain refuses further appends with that error, never with LeafAlreadyWritten, until it is reopened.
A second backend satisfying BACKENDS.md reports its own uncertain write under a distinct name, never as LeafAlreadyWritten.
